stories.title: One Year After Hurricane Melissa: Recovery Continues Across the Caribbean
stories.body:
The Salvation Army's Commitment Endures Long After the Storm

One year ago, Hurricane Melissa tore through parts of the Caribbean, leaving families, homes and communities across Jamaica, Haiti and Cuba facing widespread devastation. As residents prepared for the storm's arrival, The Salvation Army was already on the ground helping vulnerable communities prepare for what lay ahead.

Today, one year later, that commitment remains unchanged.

From emergency food distributions and shelter support to home repairs, education assistance and community rebuilding projects, The Salvation Army has stood alongside survivors every step of the recovery journey, helping thousands of families move from crisis toward stability.

Donate today to help families recover from Hurricane Melissa.

Preparing Communities Before the Storm

Before Hurricane Melissa made landfall, Salvation Army teams worked across affected communities to help residents prepare and stay safe. In Jamaica, officers, staff and volunteers encouraged residents to move to government-designated shelters, including individuals experiencing homelessness who regularly receive support through Salvation Army outreach programs.

The Salvation Army Team Emergency Radio Network (SATERN) also activated its international emergency communications system, helping distribute critical weather and emergency information to communities that may not have had access to traditional communication channels.

Responding When It Mattered Most

Because of its long-standing presence in the region, The Salvation Army was able to respond immediately after the storm passed.

Working alongside local teams and international personnel from Australia, Canada, England, Iceland and the United States, emergency relief operations delivered food, water, hygiene supplies and other essentials to families facing immense loss.

In Jamaica alone, The Salvation Army provided:

  • More than 10,000 food parcels
  • 66,300 cooked meals
  • 133,110 meal kits
  • 33,000 hygiene items
  • 6,900 care parcels containing essentials such as flashlights, blankets and socks

Additional assistance included clothing, baby supplies, cleaning products, paper goods, tarps and tents to help families meet their most urgent needs.

The response also benefited from strong partnerships across the humanitarian and private sectors. Organizations including Convoy of Hope, Greater Good Charities, GlobalMedic, Operation Blessing, Food For The Poor, Rotary Club, Khalsa Aid and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints helped expand relief efforts. The Salvation Army also worked alongside World Central Kitchen and Mercy Chefs to provide meals and other critical support.

To help reconnect isolated communities, Starlink satellite units provided through partners were installed in affected areas, restoring vital communications and internet access. Throughout the response, officers, volunteers and mission partners also offered emotional and spiritual care to individuals coping with loss and uncertainty.

In Haiti, emergency food and hygiene assistance helped families address immediate needs in the wake of the disaster. Meanwhile, in eastern Cuba, rapid-response efforts delivered food, drinking water, hygiene kits and household essentials, helping communities begin the difficult process of rebuilding.

Stories from the Recovery

Investing in Long-Term Recovery

While emergency relief was essential, recovery did not end when immediate needs were met.

Over the past year, The Salvation Army has focused on helping families rebuild their homes, restore stability and create a stronger foundation for the future.

In Jamaica, 310 households are receiving hardware store vouchers to purchase essential building materials such as roofing supplies and windows. By allowing families to determine their most urgent repair needs, the program provides greater flexibility and dignity while ensuring assistance reflects each household's unique circumstances.

The approach also supports local economic recovery by directing resources through community businesses and suppliers.

Recognizing the impact disasters have on children and education, The Salvation Army is also helping students return to the classroom. Families have received vouchers for school uniforms and supplies, reducing financial barriers while giving parents the freedom to select the items best suited to their children's needs.

In some of the hardest-hit communities, The Salvation Army is restoring school greenhouses and providing agricultural resources that support school feeding programs. These efforts help schools resume meal production, improve food security and support educational continuity for vulnerable students.

A Promise Kept

Hurricane Melissa may have passed a year ago, but for many families, recovery is still underway.

The Salvation Army's work across Jamaica, Haiti and Cuba reflects a commitment that extends beyond immediate disaster relief. It is a promise to walk alongside communities for the long term, helping families rebuild homes, restore livelihoods and regain hope.

One year later, that work continues. Thanks to the generosity of supporters around the world, The Salvation Army remains alongside those affected by Hurricane Melissa, helping communities recover today while building resilience for tomorrow.

stories.title: Building Safer Futures in Rio's Favelas
stories.body:
In Rio de Janeiro's favela communities, The Salvation Army is helping children and families build safer, stronger futures. Through the Nova Divinéia Project, 79 children and adolescents and 64 families receive education, sports, life-skills development, psychosocial support and child-protection services designed to help young people thrive despite the challenges around them.

The impact is evident both in the lives of participating children and in the families who support them. An independent evaluation found that 89 percent of surveyed families reported improvements in their children's development and behavior. Children who once struggled with confidence, participation and communication are growing into more engaged learners, stronger teammates and emerging leaders within their peer groups.

This work is taking place in communities where poverty, violence, drug trafficking and exploitation can put childhood at risk. For decades, The Salvation Army Brazil has walked alongside families in Rio's favelas, creating safe spaces where children can learn, develop healthy relationships and discover opportunities for a brighter future. Today, that commitment continues while expanding to reach even more vulnerable young people across the city.

Helping Children Grow and Thrive

The Nova Divinéia Project serves children and adolescents ages 6 to 17 through a structured program focused on personal development, family support and community participation. Currently, the project supports 49 children between the ages of 6 and 11 and 30 adolescents ages 12 to 14, while engaging 64 families in the process.

Participants take part in sports, educational activities, arts and cultural programs, life-skills development and psychosocial support. Children and young people also receive daily nutrition and individualized follow-up designed to help them overcome challenges and reach their full potential.

Children who initially struggled with concentration, confidence and group participation are now communicating more effectively, working collaboratively and taking greater responsibility for their personal development.

Many participants have become more confident speaking in front of groups, sharing ideas and engaging with their peers. Others have emerged as informal leaders, helping classmates understand activities and encouraging participation from younger children. Children who were once hesitant to engage are increasingly participating in activities and building stronger relationships with those around them.

Creating Alternatives to Risk

The work is especially important because of the environment in which it takes place.

Nova Divinéia operates in a favela community where children and adolescents are regularly exposed to the influence of drug trafficking, violence and exploitation. Criminal groups often target young people with promises of easy money, status and power, while sexual abuse and other forms of violence remain persistent threats.

The Salvation Army's response is rooted in prevention, protection and opportunity.

Children participate in activities designed to strengthen social skills, build confidence and develop healthy relationships. Workshops help young people understand their rights, learn about personal safety and develop strategies for navigating difficult situations. Through sports including soccer, volleyball, karate, jiu-jitsu and capoeira, participants develop teamwork, discipline and resilience.

Each child follows an Individual Development Plan, allowing staff to monitor progress and provide personalized support. Families are also engaged through regular follow-up, guidance and referrals to services when additional assistance is needed.

Strengthening Families and Communities

The Nova Divinéia Project extends far beyond the children enrolled in the program. Family visits, counseling and community outreach help strengthen the support systems surrounding vulnerable children. Staff work closely with parents and caregivers to address challenges, improve family relationships and connect households with available services.

Community engagement has also become an important part of the project's impact. During Brazil's national campaign to combat sexual abuse and exploitation of children and adolescents, The Salvation Army organized a community action event that reached approximately 162 people. Residents accessed services including vaccinations, eye examinations, legal support, civil-defense workshops and assistance obtaining official documentation.

The project also plays an active role in advocating for children's rights. Through participation in the Municipal Council for the Rights of Children and Adolescents, The Salvation Army has contributed to the development of local public policies affecting vulnerable children and families. These efforts helped secure approval to raise R$275,000 for initiatives aimed at preventing sexual violence against children, while additional proposals focused on child labor prevention are being developed.

Expanding the Impact to Ramos

Building on the success of Nova Divinéia, The Salvation Army is preparing to expand its work into Ramos, another neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro's North Zone.

A recent feasibility study identified significant needs among local adolescents and young adults, including educational gaps and limited access to structured sports, cultural, leisure and employment-preparation opportunities outside school hours. The study recommended the development of social-assistance services tailored to vulnerable young people and their families.

Preparatory work is already underway. Local Salvation Army leaders have established connections with community partners and social-assistance services, while plans are in place to recruit additional staff and complete the legal registrations required to begin operations.

Once launched, the Ramos initiative will build on the proven experience of Nova Divinéia by providing structured socio-educational support, strengthening family and community ties and creating safer pathways for adolescents and young adults.

Across Rio's favelas, The Salvation Army is helping young people build confidence, strengthen relationships and discover opportunities that can change the course of their future. Through consistent care, trusted community partnerships and a commitment to protecting children, lives are being transformed one child, one family and one community at a time.

A Family's Story of Transformation

One family's experience demonstrates how holistic support can create lasting change.

An 11-year-old girl joined the project while struggling with grief, anxiety and family challenges following the violent death of a relative. According to her mother, she had become withdrawn, irritable and reluctant to communicate. The family also faced strained relationships and concerns about the child's safety in a community affected by armed confrontations.

The Salvation Army responded through a combination of psychosocial support, family guidance, home visits and referrals for psychological care.

Over time, the girl's mother reported significant changes. Her daughter became happier, more communicative and eager to attend activities. She began sharing what she learned about respect, emotions, personal safety and children's rights. Family relationships improved, and the child developed a stronger sense of confidence and security.

The support extended beyond the child. Following guidance and referrals, the mother sought psychological support herself. She reported improvements in her emotional well-being, healthier family relationships and positive lifestyle changes that benefited the entire household.

The story illustrates a core principle of The Salvation Army's approach: when children receive support, the positive impact often extends to the whole family.

Help a Child Build a Safer Future

Your support helps The Salvation Army provide safe spaces, education, mentorship and protection for children growing up in Rio's favelas, creating opportunities that can change the course of a life.

stories.title: One Month After Nepal's Floods, The Salvation Army Continues Supporting Families
stories.body:
One month after devastating floods swept through communities in northern Nepal, The Salvation Army has provided emergency food, clothing and essential household supplies to 170 affected families as they begin the long process of recovery.

The floods, triggered by a sudden surge in the Bhotekoshi River on 26 August, left widespread destruction across multiple districts, washing away homes, businesses, roads and bridges and leaving thousands of people displaced. In response, The Salvation Army Nepal Region quickly mobilized to support survivors with basic essentials and emergency relief.

Working in close coordination with local and national authorities, Salvation Army teams traveled to some of the hardest-hit areas, including Syabrubesi in Rasuwa District, where entire communities were devastated by the floodwaters. Reaching affected families required navigating damaged roads and challenging terrain, but relief teams successfully delivered urgently needed supplies to those most impacted.

A total of 170 families received food and household relief packages containing rice, lentils, cooking oil, noodles and fiber quilts. The assistance helped meet immediate needs for families who had lost homes, possessions and sources of income in the disaster.

Recognizing the particular challenges facing children, The Salvation Army also provided 160 sets of clothing, including T-shirts and trousers, for distribution to boys and girls whose belongings had been destroyed by the flooding.

As teams distributed aid and assessed ongoing needs, they encountered stories of profound loss. In communities such as Betrawati, survivors described returning to find homes, businesses and farmland buried beneath mud and debris. Many families lost loved ones, while others have been forced to relocate as they wait for opportunities to rebuild their lives.

The Salvation Army also provided basic essentials beyond relief distributions. During assessment visits, staff assisted vulnerable survivors, including helping a mother and her infant travel to Kathmandu to access medical treatment.

While emergency relief has provided vital support, recovery efforts are only beginning. Communities along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors continue to face significant challenges, including the loss of housing, livelihoods and access to essential services. Many families now require temporary shelter, household items and educational support for children whose schooling has been disrupted.

The Salvation Army Nepal Region is planning a second phase of assistance and continuing assessments in partnership with local authorities and community stakeholders. Future support is expected to include winterization assistance and longer-term recovery initiatives to help families rebuild safe and stable lives.

Through emergency relief and ongoing recovery efforts, The Salvation Army remains committed to standing alongside flood-affected communities in Nepal, offering practical support and hope as families work to recover from this devastating disaster.

stories.title: As Ebola Spreads in Eastern DRC, The Salvation Army Expands Prevention and Education Efforts
stories.body:
With cases increasing and the outbreak spreading into new districts, The Salvation Army is expanding community education, hygiene promotion and infection prevention efforts across the Democratic Republic of Congo, reaching schools, corps, health facilities and vulnerable communities with life-saving information.

The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to grow at an alarming pace. Since May, confirmed cases have risen sharply, with the virus now affecting multiple provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uélé.

While government authorities and health partners continue to strengthen surveillance, treatment capacity and contact tracing, one challenge remains clear: communities need trusted information and practical guidance to help prevent the disease from spreading further.

For The Salvation Army, that means extending prevention efforts deep into affected regions and at-risk communities.

Taking Prevention to Communities

Earlier phases of The Salvation Army's response focused on strengthening readiness within health facilities, providing protective equipment and training healthcare workers in infection prevention measures.

Now, as the outbreak spreads into new districts, the organization is broadening its efforts to reach communities across eastern DRC with education, awareness and hygiene initiatives designed to slow transmission before infections occur.

New projects under development will support large-scale community awareness-raising campaigns, expanded WASH (water, sanitation and hygiene) activities, and practical infection prevention measures in communities facing heightened risk.

This approach reflects a growing recognition that Ebola cannot be contained through medical interventions alone. Communities must understand how the disease spreads, how to reduce risk and when to seek help.

Reaching Communities Through Schools and Corps

A key strength of The Salvation Army's response is its ability to work through existing community networks that already reach thousands of people every week.

New initiatives will expand awareness campaigns throughout Salvation Army schools, corps and community programs, ensuring that teachers, officers, Salvationists, students and families receive accurate information and practical guidance on Ebola prevention.

School-based projects will integrate hygiene promotion, infection prevention and community awareness activities, helping young people become trusted messengers within their families and communities.

At the same time, corps-based initiatives will equip local officers and leaders to share life-saving information through worship services, community gatherings and existing outreach ministries.

By bringing together education, health and mission efforts[PM1] The Salvation Army is pursuing an integrated approach that extends trusted information far beyond health facilities and into communities where misinformation and fear can undermine response efforts.

Supporting a Locally Led Response

The Salvation Army's early work has already been recognized by the Congolese Ministry of Health, which publicly thanked the organization for its leadership in community awareness-raising and training efforts. Salvation Army health personnel have also participated in specialist coordination meetings and received additional training to strengthen local response capacity.

The organization's growing role reflects the importance of trusted local institutions during public health emergencies. In areas where communities may be hesitant to engage with outside agencies, local officers, teachers, health workers and faith leaders are often best positioned to build understanding and encourage protective behaviors.

Powered by Partnership

The expansion of these prevention and awareness efforts is being made possible, in part, through support from UPS.

UPS funding is helping The Salvation Army strengthen its ability to educate communities, expand hygiene and infection prevention activities, and reach more people through its network of schools, corps and community-based programs.

As the outbreak continues to evolve, this support is helping ensure that communities receive accurate information, practical resources and trusted guidance before the virus gains further ground.

While treatment and emergency response remain vital, prevention remains one of the most effective tools available. Through partnerships like UPS and the dedication of local Salvation Army teams across the DRC, thousands more people will have access to the information they need to protect themselves, their families and their communities.

stories.title: Life in Ukraine, Years into War
stories.body:
Years into the war, daily life for families across Ukraine is shaped by hardship, disruption, and the strain of uncertainty. Millions have been displaced, including approximately 3.7 million people displaced within Ukraine and a further 5.9 million forced to seek refuge in neighboring countries. Homes have been damaged or destroyed, and civilians continue to be injured by attacks. Families live with the ongoing impact of repeated exposure to air strikes and violence. Household savings have run out, employment remains unstable, and rising costs for food, rent, and utilities continue to erode purchasing power. Children, older adults, and people living with disabilities are among those most affected, often with limited capacity to recover under sustained pressure.

Families continue to adapt to repeated disruption in daily routines. Schooling is interrupted, sleep is inconsistent, and household stability is difficult to maintain over time. Millions of children have experienced ongoing trauma and disruption to their education, while access to consistent support services, including safe spaces and psychological care, remains limited in many communities.

In response, The Salvation Army World Service Office (SAWSO) continues to support the delivery of community-based assistance through eight locations across Ukraine. While many organizations have scaled back operations, local teams have remained in place, maintaining a continuous presence for families navigating prolonged crisis conditions.

Through these programs, The Salvation Army provides targeted support for households directly affected by conflict, including those displaced or impacted by active fighting. Current services focus on addressing sustained, everyday pressures families face:

  • Food voucher assistance delivered monthly across seven locations, supporting households directly affected by the conflict, including those displaced or impacted by active fighting
  • After-school programs providing daily meals, educational support, and access to professional psychological care for children
  • Ongoing support for local staff and volunteers working under prolonged operational pressure

This work reflects a distinctly people-centered approach, focused on dignity and the time required to understand individual circumstances and respond accordingly. In many locations, support extends to those with the least mobility and fewest alternatives, including older adults living alone, people with disabilities, and households facing long-term displacement.

The population surveyed is highly vulnerable: 90% reported displacement, 56% reported a household member with functional difficulty or disability, 52% had children in the household, and 38% of respondents were over the age of 60.

Data collected through Salvation Army programs in Ukraine, drawing from more than 3,500 survey responses, indicates sustained and significant need among households receiving assistance. Ninety percent of households are living below the poverty line, and 94 percent report that they are unable to meet basic household needs. Nearly half of all respondents report skipping meals to make ends meet, reflecting limited capacity for recovery under prolonged crisis conditions.

Across Ukraine, Salvation Army food voucher programs are delivered monthly through seven locations, reflecting sustained, and growing, need over time. Recent program data shows:

  • 90% of people receiving the vouchers live below the poverty line
  • 94% report they are unable to meet basic household needs such as buying food and medicines
  • 49% of people receiving the vouchers report skipping meals to make ends meet

These figures reflect conditions in which food assistance is an essential part of daily survival - the difference between eating and not eating.

Many recipients are older adults or individuals living with disabilities, with limited ability to increase income or recover economically. Fixed pensions, rising food costs, and ongoing displacement have steadily reduced purchasing power, leaving households with few viable alternatives.

For those who have relocated, finding stable work remains difficult. Employment options are limited, and income is often insufficient to meet rising costs. For others, prolonged exposure to stress, displacement, or injury has affected their ability to work at all.

In this context, food vouchers allow households to make limited resources stretch further. Vouchers are redeemed through local shops, allowing recipients to choose food and basic goods that meet dietary and health needs while supporting local markets. For many, this flexibility is critical in balancing food with essential costs such as rent, utilities, and medication.

As humanitarian funding has declined and other programs have narrowed, demand for food assistance has continued to increase. The Salvation Army's ongoing presence has required maintaining regular distributions while responding to growing need among those with the fewest alternatives.

Read more about The Salvation Army's food voucher and food distribution programs to support Ukrainian Refugees

A significant proportion of displaced households include children experiencing ongoing disruption to learning, alongside persistent signs of psychological stress. Program staff report patterns including behavioral withdrawal, difficulty concentrating, and declining academic performance - conditions that require consistent, professional support over time.

Access to mental health care remains limited. Families consistently report that private psychological services are unaffordable, particularly as household budgets are increasingly absorbed by essential costs. For Ukrainian families, the services provided through The Salvation Army's after-school programs are one of the only places where psychological care is accessible.

Across Ukraine, children are growing up under conditions of sustained instability.

Displacement, interrupted education, economic pressure, and repeated exposure to insecurity have contributed to persistent stress responses that do not resolve without structured, professional support. Program staff consistently report patterns including behavioral withdrawal, difficulty concentrating, and declining academic performance. These are ongoing conditions that do not resolve on their own over time and require sustained, professional intervention rather than short-term or informal support.

Access to free mental health care for children remains limited across Ukraine. Families consistently report that private psychological services are unaffordable, particularly as household budgets are increasingly absorbed by food, rent, and utilities. For families already unable to meet basic household needs, this type of support would otherwise remain out of reach. In many communities, Salvation Army afterschool programs are among the only accessible sources of professional psychological support for children.

Afterschool programs are delivered through corps facilities and are designed to integrate educational, material, and psychosocial components rather than treating mental health needs in isolation. Core elements include:

  • A hot daily meal
  • Structured routines and group activities
  • Homework and learning support with professional teachers
  • Ongoing access to trained psychologists

This integrated approach reflects field experience indicating that psychological support is most effective when delivered alongside stability in daily structure and basic material support. It also reflects the importance of supporting children as families and communities look toward longer-term recovery.

Read more about The Salvation Army's after-school program and psychological support services

At the same time, food assistance has become a central part of daily survival for many households. As income options diminish and prices rise, food vouchers are no longer supplemental but essential. Delivered monthly and redeemable through local shops, they allow families to prioritize basic nutrition while managing other fixed costs such as rent, utilities, and medication.

As humanitarian funding has declined and other programs have narrowed, demand for support continues to increase. The Salvation Army's sustained presence has required adapting to changing conditions while maintaining consistent service delivery to those most in need.

Read more about how Salvation Army scouts deliver food and support to isolated households in Ukraine

The stories that follow offer a closer look at what this prolonged crisis means for individuals and communities. They reflect everyday realities rather than extraordinary moments: families stretching food vouchers, children learning to process trauma, and local staff carrying on their work amid ongoing disruption.

Together, they show how consistent, community-based support, provided by The Salvation Army, continues to provide stability for families, children, and older adults who are navigating prolonged uncertainty with limited alternatives. Humanitarian need in Ukraine for some time now is no longer about emergency response. It's about sustaining daily life in the face of overwhelming odds.

stories.title: The Salvation Army Responds Following Devastating Floods in Nepal
stories.body:
The Salvation Army is preparing to provide emergency relief to flood-affected families on the nepal-tibet border.

The Salvation Army is mobilizing emergency assistance for families affected by catastrophic flooding along the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal, where a sudden flash flood near the Nepal-China border has left hundreds dead or missing and caused widespread destruction across multiple districts.

Triggered by an avalanche that blocked a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, the flood struck with little warning on August 26, sweeping away homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure. Communities in some of the hardest-hit areas remain difficult to access due to damaged transportation routes and disrupted communications.

In response, The Salvation Army's Nepal Region, working through the India Eastern Territory, is preparing to provide emergency relief to approximately 300 flood-affected families, reaching an estimated 1,500 people in Nuwakot District.

Relief efforts will focus on meeting immediate needs, including:

  • Food packages and safe drinking water
  • Essential household items such as blankets, bedding and emergency lights
  • Hygiene supplies including soap, towels and other sanitation items

The Salvation Army is coordinating with district and municipal authorities to identify the most vulnerable families and ensure assistance reaches those with the greatest need. Local officers, staff, corps members and volunteers will support the distribution effort.

"The Salvation Army is committed to providing immediate, practical and compassionate assistance to those affected by this disaster," local leaders said. "Our goal is to help families meet their most urgent needs while beginning the difficult process of recovery."

Emergency response activities are expected to begin in the coming days as access to affected communities becomes available.

Please keep the people of Nepal, first responders and all those impacted by this disaster in your prayers.

stories.title: The Salvation Army Responds Following Deadly Earthquake in Colombia
stories.body:
The Salvation Army is mobilizing emergency assistance following a powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on August 10, causing widespread destruction and loss of life across multiple regions of the country.

According to initial reports, more than 250 people have died and thousands more have been injured, displaced, or otherwise affected by the disaster. Communities across Colombia's Coffee Region, including the cities of Pereira and Manizales, experienced significant damage to homes, schools, health facilities, and other critical infrastructure. Ongoing aftershocks have further complicated recovery efforts and left many families unable to return to their homes.

The Salvation Army's officers and volunteers in Colombia quickly began assessing conditions in affected communities through field visits and communication with local leaders and residents. Those assessments identified urgent needs for food, safe drinking water, hygiene supplies, and essential household items among families who have lost access to basic necessities.

To address those needs, The Salvation Army is launching an emergency response to assist 300 of the most vulnerable families in Pereira and Manizales. Relief efforts will provide food assistance, drinking water, hygiene supplies, mattresses, bedding, and other essential household items to help families meet their immediate needs while longer-term recovery efforts are established.

"The needs remain significant as communities begin the difficult process of recovery," said representatives from The Salvation Army's Latin America North Territory. "Many families have lost homes, belongings, and access to basic services. This response is focused on helping people meet their most urgent needs during the critical weeks following the earthquake."

The Salvation Army Corps in Armenia, Quindío, located approximately one hour from Pereira, is serving as a key operational hub for the response. Officers, staff, and volunteers are coordinating with local authorities, community leaders, and other humanitarian organizations to ensure assistance reaches those most affected and to avoid duplication of services.

Priority will be given to vulnerable households, including families with children, older adults, people with disabilities, and others facing heightened challenges as a result of the disaster.

In addition to providing practical assistance, The Salvation Army is offering pastoral care, emotional support, and encouragement to individuals and families coping with the aftermath of the earthquake.

As rescue operations continue and communities begin rebuilding, The Salvation Army remains committed to standing alongside those affected and providing support during the difficult days ahead.

stories.title: From Ukraine to the UN: Salvation Army Insights Inform Global Human Rights Review
stories.body:
Drawing on years of service alongside displaced families, The Salvation Army's experience in Ukraine is helping bring the realities of war, poverty, and displacement before the United Nations.

For more than four years, The Salvation Army has stood alongside families whose lives have been upended by the war in Ukraine. Through food assistance, educational support, mental health programs, community services, and aid for displaced families, Salvation Army personnel have witnessed firsthand the challenges facing some of the country's most vulnerable people. Today, those experiences are helping inform discussions at one of the world's most influential international forums: the United Nations

The Salvation Army's International Social Justice Commission (ISJC) recently submitted a report to the United Nations Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review (UPR), a process through which every UN member state undergoes a review of its human rights record. Alongside submissions from governments and international organizations, civil society groups are invited to contribute evidence and perspectives that help ensure the lived experiences of ordinary people are represented in global discussions.

The report on Ukraine focuses on the experiences of internally displaced people, many of whom continue to face significant barriers in accessing healthcare, education, and social protection despite legal safeguards designed to protect them. Older adults, people living with disabilities, and families caring for children often face the greatest challenges. The report also highlights the continuing impact of the war on children's education and well-being, including ongoing disruptions caused by conflict and displacement.

Read the Report on Ukraine: Rights of Internally Displaced Persons, Right to Health and Right to Education

While the report was submitted through the ISJC, its findings reflect realities The Salvation Army has encountered throughout its extensive work in Ukraine and neighboring countries since the conflict began. Across Ukraine, millions remain displaced, families continue to struggle with rising living costs, and children are growing up amid prolonged uncertainty and disruption. These are challenges that Salvation Army corps officers, staff, and volunteers encounter every day as they serve their communities.

The Salvation Army World Service Office (SAWSO) has played an important role in supporting these efforts. Through partnership with The Salvation Army's Eastern Europe Territory, SAWSO has helped sustain programs that provide practical assistance and long-term support for families navigating the realities of life during wartime. Current initiatives include food voucher programs that allow families to purchase essential goods, after-school programs that provide children with safe spaces, meals, and emotional support, and services designed to assist displaced households as they rebuild stability.

Learn More About The Salvation Army’s Work in Ukraine

The scale of the need remains significant. Millions of Ukrainians remain displaced, while many households continue to face economic hardship, limited access to services, and ongoing uncertainty about the future. At the same time, many humanitarian organizations have reduced operations as international funding declines, increasing the importance of trusted local networks that can remain embedded in the communities they serve. The Salvation Army has continued to maintain that presence, providing consistent support long after global headlines have moved elsewhere.

The submission to the United Nations represents another dimension of that commitment. Beyond meeting immediate needs, The Salvation Army is helping ensure that the voices of vulnerable people are heard by decision-makers responsible for shaping national and international responses. By bringing evidence from communities affected by conflict directly into international discussions, the organization helps connect local realities with global action.

For SAWSO, the report underscores the importance of supporting work that extends beyond humanitarian assistance alone. It reflects a broader commitment to dignity, justice, and advocacy for people whose experiences might otherwise go unheard. It also demonstrates how insights gathered through local ministry and community programs can contribute to conversations taking place on the world stage.

As Ukraine prepares for its next review before the United Nations Human Rights Council, The Salvation Army's message is clear: the challenges facing displaced families, children, older adults, and people with disabilities must not be overlooked. Through both practical service and international advocacy, The Salvation Army remains committed to standing alongside those affected by conflict and helping ensure their experiences help shape the solutions of tomorrow.

Key Facts from the Report

The Salvation Army's Presence in Ukraine

  • The Salvation Army has served communities in Ukraine since 1994 and now operates in eight locations across the country.

Evidence Submitted to the United Nations

  • The report draws on data collected from 3,823 conflict-affected individuals participating in Salvation Army-supported programs.
  • Findings were gathered through surveys, interviews, and beneficiary feedback across multiple humanitarian initiatives.

Poverty and Economic Hardship

  • 91% of survey respondents reported household incomes below the World Bank poverty line.
  • 98% said they were unable to fully meet their household's basic needs.
  • Many families reported borrowing money, reducing food consumption, delaying rent payments, or relying on relatives and friends for support.

Children and Education

  • The Salvation Army's After School Project supported 323 children in 2025 and indirectly benefited 601 parents and caregivers.
  • According to UNICEF, children in frontline areas have spent between 3,000 and 5,000 hours in shelters during air raid alerts since the conflict began.
  • Salvation Army after-school programs provide educational support, psychosocial care, and safe spaces equipped with bomb shelters.

Health and Vulnerable Populations

  • 42% of survey respondents were age 60 or older.
  • 54% of households included someone experiencing mobility, vision, hearing, memory, or other functional limitations.
  • Older adults and people with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to healthcare access.

Why It Matters

  • The Salvation Army's findings were submitted to the United Nations Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, helping ensure the experiences of internally displaced and conflict-affected Ukrainians are reflected in international human rights discussions.

stories.title: Restoring Dignity and Hope for Women Living with HIV in India
stories.body:
When a woman in southern India loses her husband, the loss can extend far beyond grief. For many widows living with HIV, it also means losing financial security, social standing, and sometimes even the support of family and community members.

Stigma surrounding HIV often leaves women isolated at the exact moment they need help most. Many are left to care for children alone while managing a chronic illness, navigating poverty, and worrying about how they will provide for their family's future.

This was the reality facing hundreds of women across 190 villages in Tamil Nadu, India, before The Salvation Army's Integrated Health Initiative began its work.

The project focused on one of the most vulnerable groups in the region: widows living with HIV and AIDS and their children. While access to life-saving antiretroviral treatment has improved in India, many women still struggle to remain healthy because of poor nutrition, lack of transportation to medical facilities, financial hardship, and limited community support. Children in these households often face their own challenges, including interrupted education, social isolation, and uncertain futures.

Rather than addressing a single need, the initiative recognized that health, education, economic stability, and social acceptance are deeply connected.

Through regular home visits, counseling, medical support, and partnerships with government health services, women were encouraged and supported to remain on HIV treatment. The results were significant. Every widow enrolled in the program remained connected to treatment, helping women maintain their health, care for their families, and continue participating in daily life.

Improved health created opportunities for something equally important: independence.

Many participants were supported in developing small businesses and income-generating activities ranging from tailoring and livestock rearing to petty trade and other microenterprises. Access to self-help groups, financial literacy training, and microcredit opened doors that had previously been closed. Women who once relied on others for survival began earning income, managing household finances, and making plans for the future.

At the same time, the project invested in the next generation.

More than 100 children from HIV-affected households received educational support to help them remain in school. Scholarships, school supplies, and life-skills training eased the financial burden on families while helping children build confidence and resilience. For mothers already carrying the weight of illness and poverty, knowing their children could continue their education represented a powerful source of hope.

Yet some of the project's most meaningful outcomes are harder to measure.

Many widows entered the program carrying not only economic burdens, but emotional ones. Years of discrimination and exclusion had eroded confidence and self-worth. Through training, counseling, and participation in community groups, women began rebuilding that confidence. They gained a better understanding of their rights, strengthened relationships within their communities, and developed the courage to advocate for themselves and their children.

Community attitudes changed as well. Awareness efforts helped reduce misconceptions about HIV and encouraged greater compassion and understanding. Women who had once been marginalized found increasing acceptance and support from neighbors, community leaders, and local networks.

Today, the impact of the project continues long after funding has ended. Women remain connected to government health services and social protection programs. Small businesses continue to generate income. Children remain in school. Self-help groups provide ongoing support and encouragement.

Most importantly, women who were once defined by illness, loss, and stigma are increasingly defined by something else: resilience.

The Integrated Health Initiative demonstrates what is possible when support extends beyond immediate needs and invests in the whole person. By strengthening health, livelihoods, education, and social inclusion together, the project helped create lasting change for women living with HIV and the families who depend on them.

For many participants, the journey did not simply lead to better health. It led to renewed dignity, greater independence, and the confidence to envision a different future.

stories.title: Creating Better Spaces for Children to Learn, Grow and Thrive in Costa Rica
stories.body:
A partnership between Rotary and SAWSO IN COSTA RICA is improving educational spaces, creating stronger opportunities for children to learn, grow, and thrive.

For years, staff at CIDAI León XIII in San José, Costa Rica, worked around challenges that most schools shouldn't have to face. A leaking roof disrupted learning during heavy rains. Restroom facilities needed significant improvements. Teachers and caregivers did their best to create a safe, welcoming environment, but they knew their children deserved better.

Today, thanks to the generosity of the Brooklyn Rotary Club through SAWSO, that vision has become a reality.

A recently completed renovation project transformed key areas of the center, creating brighter, safer, and healthier spaces for more than 120 children who attend CIDAI León XIII. The improvements included new child-friendly restroom facilities, upgraded staff facilities, and a renovated classroom with a new roof, better lighting, and improved ventilation.

The changes are about much more than buildings. Children now learn and grow in classrooms designed to support their development. Teachers and caregivers can focus on providing quality education and care in a healthier, more functional environment. Parents have renewed confidence knowing their children are spending their days in a safe and welcoming place.

"This donation represents far more than financial support," said Arlen Coulson, Administrative Assistant at CIDAI León XIII. "It fulfilled a dream that had remained unrealized for more than six years. It provides safety for our children, better hygiene, peace of mind for our teachers and, most importantly, allows more children to remain in a safe, bright, and welcoming environment that promotes learning, growth, and development."

The impact extends beyond the classroom. More than 200 families in the León XIII community will benefit from these improvements for years to come, helping ensure children have a healthy foundation for learning, growth, and a brighter future.

Thank you to the Brooklyn Rotary Club for making this project possible and for investing in the children, families, and future of León XIII. Your generosity is creating lasting change where it matters most.

stories.title: Salvation Army teams are providing relief and support in communities affected by Venezuela's deadly earthquakes
stories.body:
Local Salvation Army teams from across Venezuela are now on the ground in Caracas and are delivering help and supplies to relieve in communities affected by two powerful earthquakes that struck on 24 June.

Recovery Needs Grow as The Salvation Army Expands Support

More than five weeks after the devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela on June 24, The Salvation Army and its partners continue to provide practical support, emotional care and recovery assistance to communities facing an uncertain future.

The humanitarian crisis remains severe. According to the latest official figures, 5,546 people have died, more than 16,700 have been injured, and nearly 24,000 people are still living in temporary camps. Authorities report that 856 buildings were damaged, including 190 that collapsed completely. Since the initial earthquakes, approximately 1,500 aftershocks have been recorded, compounding the challenges facing affected communities.

While emergency needs remain significant, conversations with residents increasingly point to longer-term concerns. Many families continue to live in temporary accommodations while facing uncertainty about housing, income and the recovery process.

Salvation Army Response Continues

Operating in partnership with Emmanuel Church and local volunteers, The Salvation Army remains actively engaged in relief efforts across affected communities.

The Salvation Army response has reached 7,134 people with food, water, hygiene supplies, bedding, clothing, emotional care and spiritual support.

Relief efforts have included:

  • 3,116 meals provided to people affected by the earthquake
  • 1,006 food parcels distributed to families and communities in need
  • 1,387 hygiene, cleaning and essential care kits provided to families
  • 305 distributions of basic medicines and health supplies provided
  • Mattresses, pillows, bedsheets and clothing distributed to support displaced families

The Salvation Army has also continued to support those working tirelessly in response and recovery operations. Small care packages containing drinks, energy bars, hand sanitizer and wipes have been distributed to rescue workers, and 23 safety helmets have been supplied for those involved in rubble removal efforts.

Caring for More Than Physical Needs

Alongside practical support, emotional and spiritual care remains a key part of The Salvation Army's ministry.

Response teams have held more than 400 individual conversations with people affected by the disaster, offering encouragement, prayer and support where appropriate. Children's activities and psychosocial support events have also provided moments of normalcy and joy for young people living in shelters, with hundreds of children participating in programs organized during the response.

Looking Ahead

As recovery needs grow, The Salvation Army is planning for the next phase of assistance. Current efforts include developing longer-term recovery projects, strengthening logistics and transportation capacity, and preparing for continued support in the months ahead.

After weeks of intensive field work, team members recently took a brief weekend respite before returning to ongoing response operations. Despite challenging living conditions and long days in the field, preparations continue to ensure assistance can be sustained and expanded as needs evolve.

The Salvation Army remains committed to standing alongside the people of Venezuela for as long as needed, providing practical support, compassionate care and hope to communities rebuilding after disaster.

Salvation Army expands support for earthquake survivors and frontline rescue workers in Venezuela

More than three weeks after devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela, Salvation Army teams and local partners continue to adapt their response to meet evolving needs in affected communities.

As search and recovery efforts continue across parts of Caracas and La Guaira, thousands of families remain displaced or are waiting for news about missing loved ones. Salvation Army personnel, volunteers, and church partners are providing practical assistance alongside emotional and spiritual care for survivors, family members, and first responders working in difficult conditions.

One of the Salvation Army’s most important partnerships has been with local churches that are preparing meals for communities affected by the disaster. Because many families remain without access to kitchens or cooking facilities, churches are cooking and distributing between 300 and 500 meals each day using ingredients supplied through the response effort.

Salvation Army teams are also supporting rescue workers engaged in ongoing search operations. Assistance has included food parcels, energy snacks, refreshments, bedding items, hygiene supplies, and protective equipment such as safety helmets for volunteer responders working in hazardous conditions.

Across affected neighborhoods, Salvation Army personnel and volunteers continue to offer emotional and spiritual care to people coping with trauma, grief, and uncertainty. Team members regularly spend time listening to survivors and family members, offering encouragement, prayer when requested, and compassionate support during an extraordinarily difficult period.

Response activities continue in partnership with churches, community organizations, and humanitarian partners. While logistics and coordination remain challenging, these local relationships are helping ensure assistance reaches communities with urgent unmet needs.

As of July 15, Salvation Army-supported activities had provided:

  • 1,905 meals
  • 843 food parcels
  • 627 hygiene kits
  • 396 emotional and spiritual care conversations
  • Assistance to 5,139 individuals

In addition to support provided through local church networks, assistance is being strengthened through partnerships with UPS, Greater Good Charities, Airlink, Convoy of Hope, and other humanitarian partners, helping expand food assistance, critical relief supplies, logistics support, and emergency aid for earthquake-affected families and first responders.

The Salvation Army remains committed to serving communities affected by the disaster and adapting assistance as needs continue to evolve.

How You Can Help

Please continue praying for families who have lost loved ones, those still awaiting news of missing relatives, and the rescue workers, volunteers, churches, and humanitarian teams serving affected communities.

Financial contributions help provide food assistance, hygiene supplies, emotional and spiritual care, and other critical support for families impacted by the earthquakes.

Salvation Army Teams Expand Frontline Relief as Venezuela Earthquake Response Enters Critical Next Phase

Salvation Army teams in Venezuela are continuing to expand relief efforts for families, rescue workers and communities affected by the deadly earthquakes that struck on June 24.

Working from a coordination base in Caracas, teams are purchasing, sorting, packing and distributing essential supplies while conducting ongoing assessments to identify where needs are greatest. The response is being delivered in partnership with Emanuel Church, Centro Islámico de Venezuela and Fundación a Todas Las Cosas en Común.

Across affected communities, Salvation Army personnel and volunteers are helping meet immediate needs while supporting the people leading search and rescue efforts.

Teams have provided meals, drinks and refreshments to civil protection personnel and rescue workers working long hours in difficult conditions. They have also supplied practical equipment, including helmets, head torches and gloves, for those helping clear rubble and search damaged buildings.

One Salvation Army volunteer currently serving on the front lines has been working alongside rescue crews, helping remove debris while providing refreshments and encouragement to first responders.

In Kilometro 24, a community in El Junquito, teams visited families living in temporary shelters and distributed flour, sugar, rice, canned tuna and other essential supplies. Relief workers have also unloaded and sorted donated goods, reassessed communities surrounding the church hosting the response team, and continued coordinating efforts with partner organizations operating in the area.

"In an emergency of this magnitude, needs evolve rapidly, and with many organizations responding simultaneously, effective coordination becomes both essential and challenging. Our priority is to avoid duplication of efforts while ensuring that assistance reaches communities that might otherwise be overlooked," said Ricardo Gomez, Emergency and Development Coordinator for The Salvation Army's Latin America North Territory, who is currently serving on the ground in Caracas.

Reaching Communities with the Greatest Needs

More than 2,295 people have been killed and over 11,000 injured following the earthquakes. Many families remain displaced, separated from loved ones, or living in temporary accommodation as aftershocks continue.

Widespread building collapses have left communities like La Guaira facing enormous humanitarian needs.

"La Guaira remains the area with the greatest concentration of humanitarian needs. While support is reaching the area, the scale of the destruction is so significant that existing assistance is still insufficient," said Gomez.

Communities in central Caracas are also facing significant shortages of food, safe drinking water and hygiene supplies. Salvation Army teams continue to map needs and identify communities that may not yet be receiving adequate assistance.

Access remains a challenge. Government restrictions continue around the most heavily affected areas where search-and-rescue operations are underway. Through its partnership with Emanuel Church, which has authorization to operate in restricted zones, The Salvation Army has been able to support ongoing relief efforts while pursuing additional access for its own personnel and resources.

Movement across Caracas has also been complicated by road closures, transportation shortages and ongoing seismic activity. Following a 4.1 magnitude tremor on July 1, teams continue operating under heightened alert while monitoring aftershocks that could further affect communities and infrastructure.

Recovery Will Take Time

Alongside physical assistance, Salvation Army teams are providing emotional and spiritual support to people coping with grief, uncertainty and displacement.

While emergency relief remains the immediate focus, response leaders are also looking ahead to the long-term recovery families will face. Many families remain outdoors or in temporary shelters because their homes are unsafe.

"For most affected families, the road to recovery remains long, and our assessments continue to evolve as we learn more each day," said Gomez.

The Salvation Army continues to coordinate with local and international partners, participate in humanitarian planning groups, and assess how it can best support recovery efforts in the months ahead. Early discussions include transitional shelter solutions, vocational training opportunities and support for larger temporary shelters expected to expand as recovery efforts continue.

"Our officers, volunteers and Salvation Army members have been actively deployed in the areas affected by the recent building collapses. Today, more than ever, we reaffirm our commitment to serve without discrimination and to be a beacon of hope in the midst of recovery," said Captain Edicson Sánchez, Regional Coordinator for Venezuela.

How You Can Help

The humanitarian needs remain significant and continue to evolve as assessments reach more communities.

Donations will help The Salvation Army:

  • Provide food and essential supplies to affected families
  • Support displaced people living in temporary shelters
  • Deliver emotional and spiritual care to those coping with loss and uncertainty
  • Equip frontline responders and volunteers serving in affected communities
  • Reach underserved areas where needs remain high

As the situation develops, your support will help The Salvation Army continue providing practical assistance and compassionate care to those most affected.

Donate today to help provide families with much-needed relief.

Prayer Requests

Please join The Salvation Army in praying:

  • For those who have lost loved ones and for the many families still awaiting news of missing relatives
  • For families living with uncertainty, displacement and ongoing aftershocks
  • For rescue workers, volunteers and emergency personnel serving in challenging and often dangerous conditions
  • For wisdom, protection and strength for Salvation Army teams and partner organizations responding on the ground
  • For communities beginning the long journey of recovery and rebuilding

The Salvation Army remains grateful for the prayers, generosity, and support of partners around the world as this response continues.

Salvation Army teams expand relief efforts as Venezuela earthquake death toll rises

The Salvation Army continues to expand its response in communities affected by Venezuela's devastating earthquakes, as the scale of the disaster becomes increasingly clear.

Government reports indicate more than 2,295 people have been killed, more than 11,000 injured, and over 40,000 remain missing following the twin earthquakes that struck the country on June 24. Families across affected areas continue to face displacement, uncertainty, and the ongoing threat of aftershocks.

Working from a coordination base in Caracas, Salvation Army teams are providing essential aid and emotional support to affected families while expanding outreach to underserved communities.

In recent days, teams from The Salvation Army have distributed food and essential supplies to families sheltering in El Junquito and surrounding areas. Assistance has included flour, rice, sugar, canned tuna, drinking water, hygiene items, and other necessities. Teams have also continued to assess communities, identify unmet needs, and coordinate relief efforts with local partners and other responding organizations.

Alongside support for families, The Salvation Army has been providing meals, drinks, encouragement, and emotional care to civil protection personnel and rescue teams working long hours in difficult conditions as search and recovery operations continue.

Access remains challenging throughout Caracas. Road closures, severe congestion, and ongoing restrictions around the main collapse zone continue to complicate relief efforts. Transportation challenges have intensified as some flights are now being diverted to Valencia, several hours from the team's operational base.

Despite these obstacles, The Salvation Army is strengthening coordination with humanitarian partners and are participating in United Nations coordination meetings focused on logistics, food assistance, water and sanitation, and protection services. This will help ensure aid reaches communities where needs remain greatest.

The response continues from Emmanuel Church in Caracas, where Salvation Army personnel and volunteers are working alongside local partners to support families affected by the disaster. Teams are also providing spiritual care and emotional support for individuals coping with loss, displacement, and uncertainty.

"Our officers, volunteers and Salvation Army members have been actively deployed in the areas affected by the recent building collapses," said Captain Edicson Sánchez, Regional Coordinator for Venezuela. "Today, more than ever, we reaffirm our commitment to serve without discrimination and to be a beacon of hope in the midst of recovery."

As needs continue to grow, The Salvation Army is assessing opportunities to further expand relief operations in the days ahead, while continuing to prioritize communities with the greatest unmet needs.

Needs Remain Urgent

Current priority needs include:

  • Food
  • Safe drinking water
  • Hygiene supplies
  • Diapers and other essential household items
  • Blankets and sleeping mats
  • Tarpaulins for families living in temporary conditions
  • Medical supplies through partner organizations

Donations will help The Salvation Army continue providing practical assistance, emotional support, and hope to families affected by this unfolding humanitarian crisis.

Response Underway

After a 19-hour journey across Venezuela, navigating damaged roads, debris, and restricted access, Salvation Army teams have reached Caracas and are now operating from a local church, which will be used as a distribution hub over coming weeks and months.

The Salvation Army team, made up of officers and volunteers, immediately set to work, procuring and distributing essential supplies from their base and working alongside a local partner church to reach communities with acute unmet needs. Food, hygiene supplies, basic household items, sleeping mats, and blankets are being sourced locally and delivered directly to people most severely affected.

Across impacted areas, families are sleeping outside in streets, parks, and open spaces after their homes were damaged or are no longer safe. The scale of the disaster continues to grow, with at least 920 people killed, more than 3,300 injured, and tens of thousands still missing as search and rescue operations continue. Teams are prioritizing these communities as aftershocks persist; access remains limited in some locations, and communication challenges and road damage slow efforts to reach those most in need.

Relief is being directed to communities with the most urgent needs, particularly those displaced from their homes and sleeping outside, as well as areas affected by damaged infrastructure and limited access to services.

Relief Priorities and Ongoing Needs

Teams are delivering essential supplies, sourced locally and distributed directly to families in affected communities as needs continue to grow, with ongoing aftershocks continuing to disrupt air and road access to some areas.

“The preliminary assessment shows significant needs for food, hygiene supplies, household items, sleeping mats, and blankets. Many people are sleeping outdoors due to damage to their homes, and these priorities will continue to be refined as access to affected communities improves,” said Ricardo Gomez, Emergency and Development Coordinator for The Salvation Army’s Latin America North Territory.

In addition to meeting immediate physical needs, teams are also offering emotional and spiritual support, spending time with individuals and families who have lost homes, loved ones, and a sense of security as the situation continues to unfold.

Communities across the affected region are facing urgent and evolving needs. As response efforts expand, continued support is critical to reach more people and sustain assistance in the days ahead.

How Support Makes an Impact

Support is needed to:

  • Deliver essential items such as food, hygiene supplies, and basic household goods
  • Reach communities that remain difficult to access due to damaged infrastructure
  • Maintain a sustained presence as needs increase and more areas become accessible

Donations enable The Salvation Army to respond quickly, support local teams already on the ground, and remain alongside communities as they begin the longer process of recovery.

Give Now

The Salvation Army is often among the first to respond in times of crisis, with local teams and church networks already in place, and remains long after the initial emergency phase, supporting communities through recovery and rebuilding.

stories.title: Join the Effort to Protect Communities From Ebola in DR Congo
stories.body:
With Ebola cases rising, The Salvation Army is urgently providing protective equipment, hygiene supplies, hand-washing stations, public health messaging, and support for health care facilities across four high-risk areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The Salvation Army is urgently providing critical protection and prevention measures across high-risk areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo as confirmed Ebola cases have increased by more than 30 percent in the past week to more than 800. Deaths now exceed 200.

This response is being mobilized through four targeted emergency efforts, equipping health facilities, supporting communities, and putting practical infection control measures in place where they are most urgently needed.

Transmission is continuing across multiple provinces, with Ituri Province remaining the epicenter. The outbreak has expanded into new health zones, and cases and deaths continue to be reported daily, indicating that the situation is not yet under control.

At this stage, the priority is speed. With no fully approved vaccine or specific treatment available for this strain, controlling the spread depends on ensuring that health workers and communities have consistent access to protective equipment, hygiene supplies, and infection control measures before transmission accelerates further.

What Is Happening on the Ground

Through its corps, clinics, health services, and schools, The Salvation Army is already present in the communities most affected by the outbreak, with local teams known to and trusted by the people they serve.

What is needed now is to scale resources quickly, putting protective equipment, hygiene supplies, and infection control measures in place before transmission accelerates further.

In practical terms, this means equipping 13 health facilities in Kinshasa with basic protection supplies, supporting households in Ituri with hand-washing infrastructure and hygiene materials, strengthening prevention and screening efforts in Kalemie, and ensuring that health workers and patients in North and South Kivu have consistent access to protective equipment.

How You Can Help

Your contribution helps ensure that critical protection and prevention supplies are available quickly and at scale, before transmission accelerates further. Local teams are working to secure and put the following essential materials in place:

  • Screening equipment
    • ThermoFlash thermometers for temperature checks at health facilities and community entry points ($30 each)
  • Hygiene and infection control supplies
    • Hydroalcoholic gel for hand sanitation ($4.50 per bottle)
    • Hand-washing kits for health facilities and communities ($25 per kit)
  • Protective equipment for health workers
    • Protective coveralls ($15 each)
    • Face shields ($5 each) and protective goggles ($3.50 each)
    • Surgical masks and nitrile gloves used daily in patient care ($5–$15 per set)

How Support Is Put to Work

Contributions help put essential protection and prevention measures in place across four high-risk areas:

  • Ituri Province — Supports household-level prevention, helping 200 households (approximately 1,400 people) access hygiene supplies, hand-washing facilities, and clear public health information to reduce transmission risk.
  • North Kivu and South Kivu — Helps protect frontline care by ensuring health workers and patients in Salvation Army facilities have access to protective equipment needed for safe treatment, reaching approximately 2,050 people.
  • Kinshasa — Strengthens infection control across 13 Salvation Army health facilities, helping reduce exposure risk for both medical staff and the large number of patients they serve.
  • Kalemie (Tanganyika Province) — Expands community-level prevention through sanitation, hygiene promotion, and screening, helping protect at least 3,000 people in high-risk public settings.

Donate today to help protect communities facing the threat of Ebola in DR Congo.

stories.title: Primary Health Care to Support the Growing Chikankata Community
stories.body:
Prior to 2018, reaching hospital care from Terra Nova meant setting out on foot to cover the 24-kilometer journey to seek help at Chikankata Mission Hospital. When Ireen moved to Terra Nova for marriage with her two young children, she joined a community of about 6,000 people living across remote commercial farms anchored by a coffee plantation, far from services and without reliable transport. When a child developed fever or diarrhea, the only option was to walk. The journey could take up to ten hours, often with a sick child strapped to her back. For families in other rural communities served by the mission, the distance could be as far as 35 kilometers one way.

The journey was exhausting and risky, and it required leaving early to try to arrive before dark. In the rainy season, paths narrowed as maize and grass grew tall, cutting off visibility and making it difficult to see what lay ahead. Snakes were common, and wild animals moved through the fields. Isolation itself was frightening, and the uncertainty of an approaching stranger added to the danger. "When the maize is tall and you cannot see the road in front of you, you don't know what you will meet. Anything can happen," she said.

Reaching the hospital did not mean immediate care. Often, she arrived too late to be seen that day and had to sleep overnight, rejoining the queue the next morning before beginning the long walk home.

Because the journey could stretch over several days, families in rural communities like Ireen's frequently delayed seeking care, weighing the danger of the road against the illness itself and hoping children might recover without making the trip. Routine care also fell away. Mothers did not bring children for regular weighing or growth monitoring, and early signs of illness or malnutrition were often missed. Distance not only delayed emergency care, but it also interrupted the everyday services that keep children healthy.

It was in this context that the Primary Health Care (PHC) project was established.

A project that began in 2018 and became routine practice

In 2018, the Primary Health Care (PHC) project was established to support rural clinics providing care to the approximately 55,000 people living within a 35-kilometer radius of Chikankata Mission Hospital. These communities were spread across farming areas and settlements where distance, poor roads, and the absence of transport made access to hospital care unreliable and, at times, dangerous.

At the time, rural clinics were operating under extreme pressure. In places like Terra Nova, a single clinic served a population of about 6,000 people across six commercial farms, with no nearby alternative facility. The nearest clinic was roughly 20 kilometers away, and Chikankata Mission Hospital was more than 24 kilometers from the community. For most families, reaching care meant walking long distances, often delaying treatment until illness became severe.

When Linda arrived in Terra Nova in 2011, she did so as the only nurse at the clinic. She was responsible for all outpatient services, antenatal care, HIV services, deliveries, child health monitoring, and referrals. There was no second nurse, no rotation, and no relief. "I was alone," she said. "I was doing everything."

The workload was immediate and unrelenting. The clinic managed routine illness alongside a heavy burden of HIV and sexually transmitted infections, maternal care, and childhood disease. Linda was responsible for all deliveries at the clinic, averaging around ten births each month, or approximately 120 deliveries a year, in addition to seeing patients daily for acute and chronic conditions. "You deliver the babies. You attend to the sick. You do everything," she said.

Distance added to the strain on services. Referrals to Chikankata Mission Hospital required planning and transport over long distances and managing both routine and urgent cases from a wide catchment area placed sustained pressure on a single nurse clinic model. With limited staffing, maintaining consistent coverage across routine, preventive, and acute care was a persistent challenge.

What the Primary Health Care project added

The Primary Health Care project expanded and strengthened services delivered through rural health clinics by adding structured support from Chikankata Mission Hospital and coordinated outreach. The approach was built on a clear structure:

  • Rural clinics provide frontline care, including outpatient services, antenatal care, HIV services, basic maternity care, and child health monitoring.
  • Chikankata Mission Hospital provides referral care when complications arise and services exceed the capacity of rural clinics.
  • Maternal and Child Health outreach services extend care beyond clinic walls, delivering routine services such as child weighing and growth monitoring, immunization, antenatal and postnatal followup, family planning, and medication delivery to communities that cannot regularly reach fixed clinic sites.
  • Community Health Worker outreach services provide basic health screening and followup for individuals who are not enrolled in HIV services, including routine health checks (such as vital signs monitoring), assessment and referral for common illnesses and chronic conditions, medication followup, and identification of patients requiring further care.

Linda Lombe, a registered nurse and midwife, who has served the Terra Nova community since 2011, explained the relationship between the rural clinic and the hospital: "Terra Nova is a baby for Chikankata Mission Hospital…Chikankata is our mother." When rural clinics have referrals for outpatient care, maternity complications, or emergencies, they contact Chikankata and escalate care through established pathways.

Impact of the Primary Health Care Project at Terra Nova Clinic

The Primary Health Care project strengthened the capacity of the Terra Nova rural health clinic to deliver consistent care to a large, remote population, reducing reliance on long journeys to the hospital and stabilizing routine health services over time.

"We manage HIV care here at the clinic, but when a case is complicated, Chikankata supports us. We work together so patients do not fall out of care," said Linda Lombe, Registered Nurse and Midwife, Terra Nova Clinic.

HIV and chronic care
