  • In a catchment of 6,000 people, the clinic has supported care for a large HIV affected population.
  • The clinic currently provides ongoing treatment to more than 500 people receiving antiretroviral therapy, allowing patients to access medication and followup locally rather than travelling to the hospital.
  • Routine laboratory sample transport supports continued monitoring for people on treatment, maintaining continuity of care.
  • The clinic also manages other chronic conditions, including sexually transmitted infections, alongside general outpatient care.

Maternal and child health

  • The clinic manages approximately 10 deliveries per month, equivalent to around 120 births per year, providing local access to maternity care for women who would otherwise need to travel long distances, especially if the birth was complicated. This includes 62 adolescents aged 14 to 17.
  • Routine antenatal and postnatal services are delivered at clinic level, with referral to Chikankata Mission Hospital for complicated cases.
  • Child growth monitoring is conducted regularly, supporting early identification of health and nutrition concerns.
  • Postnatal follow-up includes family planning services, with high uptake reported at the six-week postnatal visit.

Adolescent health

  • Teenage pregnancy represents a significant proportion of maternal health demand:
  • 32 percent of pregnancies in 2024
  • 33 percent of pregnancies in 2025
  • Youth focused services, including counselling and access to family planning, form part of the clinic's ongoing work.

Staffing and service continuity

  • At the outset of the PHC period, Terra Nova operated with a single nurse delivering all clinical services, including outpatient care, maternity services, HIV care, and referrals.
  • Over time, staffing increased, allowing services to be delivered more consistently across routine, preventive, and acute care.
  • Importantly, services established during the PHC project have continued beyond the end of the original project funding, including maternity care, HIV treatment, child health monitoring, and referral pathways.

Maternal and Child Health Outreach: Supporting the Wider Primary Health Care Network

Primary Health Care at Chikankata is supported by Maternal and Child Health (MCH) services based at Chikankata Mission Hospital, which coordinate outreach and continuity of care for mothers and children across the wider catchment area.

"If we do not go out to the communities, mothers will not come. Children will miss weighing and monitoring, and we will only see them when problems have already become serious," said Dadirai Simubali, Sister in Charge, Maternal and Child Health Clinic, Chikankata Mission Hospital.

Outreach is designed for communities that cannot realistically travel to the hospital. Some are located up to 35 kilometers away. To reach these areas, MCH teams operate a regular monthly outreach schedule, covering six outreach posts and multiple outreach days each month. Through these visits, routine services are delivered closer to where families live, including immunization, child weighing and growth monitoring, antenatal booking and followup, vitamin A supplementation, family planning services, and medication delivery.

Clinic activity data illustrates the scale of this work. In a single month, the MCH clinic recorded:

  • 2,075 under-five children receiving services
  • 566 family planning clients
  • Male involvement in maternal health, with about 50 men attending with partners out of 74 booked women during that period

This outreach function reinforces the Primary Health Care model by maintaining routine contact with families, supporting early identification of health needs, and reducing gaps in care that can lead to avoidable complications. It also allows Chikankata Mission Hospital to function effectively as the hub of a Primary Health Care network, supporting both rural clinics through referral care and communities directly through structured outreach.

Why the impact has continued beyond the initial program

The Primary Health Care project at Chikankata was designed as a system, not a temporary intervention. From the outset, it organized care around rural clinics as the first point of access, structured outreach for communities that could not reliably reach fixed facilities, and Chikankata Mission Hospital as the referral hub for complications and higher-level care. Rather than replacing existing services, the Primary Health Care project strengthened how they worked together, embedding referral pathways, outreach schedules, and shared responsibility for patient follow-up across the network.

That structure is why the impact did not end when the initial project phase concluded. The Primary Health Care project established a tiered, connected model in which communitybased services function as the first point of care, supported by clear referral links to Chikankata Mission Hospital as the clinical hub. Practices introduced through the project, including clinicbased HIV management with hospital support, routine maternal and child health services, outreach to hardtoreach communities, and structured referral mechanisms, became part of everyday service delivery. As a result, access to care, treatment continuity, and referral pathways established under the Primary Health Care project continue to shape how services are delivered across the Chikankata catchment area today.

"What they were doing was good, because a lot of people were being helped, and the clinic continued providing services," said Prisca Mweetwei, a registered nurse at Terra Nova Rural Health Clinic.

stories.title: Clean Water at Chikankata: A Change Felt in Daily Life
stories.body:
Donate Today to Change Lives

For Tinashe and Precious, both 17 and in their final year at the girls’ secondary school, access to water once shaped the start of every day. Before lessons began, students often left the school compound in groups to collect water from local waterpoints. Each trip could take an hour or more, depending on queues and distance, and often meant arriving late to class.

As Precious explained, “When we went to fetch water, by the time we came back, lessons had already started. It was very hard to catch up.”

Tinashe described missing entire morning sessions, adding, “If you miss the first explanation from the teacher, it is difficult to understand the rest.”

Their experience was not unique. Across the Chikankata mission and surrounding community, families relied on the same distant boreholes and streams for drinking, cooking, washing, and bathing. Water collection was time-consuming and physically demanding, and the quality of the water itself posed serious health risks.

Related Stories

Tinashe’s Story

Precious’ Story

How the Clean Water System Works

Unsafe Water, Visible Consequences

Testing of the water sources used at Chikankata confirmed significant quality concerns. According to Aubrey, the engineer responsible for the new system, “The water showed E. Coli contamination, which means it was not safe for consumption.” Elevated mineral levels were also identified, increasing the risk of longer-term kidney-related health problems.

These findings aligned closely with what health staff at Chikankata Mission Hospital were seeing in practice. The school matron noted frequent cases of stomach illness and skin irritation among students, explaining that “many of the girls were getting rashes or stomach problems linked to the water they were using.” Similar complaints were reported across the wider community, placing additional pressure on the hospital and clinics.

A New Water System

In 2025, a new water treatment plant was installed at Chikankata to address these risks. The system was designed to remove biological contamination, including E. coli, and to improve overall water quality by addressing mineral imbalance.

Today, treated water is supplied to key facilities across the mission compound, including the hospital, schools, and hostels. Further connections to most surrounding homes are now in place with a small number of remaining homes planned to be connected soon. In areas already connected, residents no longer depend on unsafe sources for daily use.

Health staff report already significant reductions in waterborne illness, skin irritation, and hygiene related complaints, reflecting improved water quality and safer access. By addressing both immediate infection risk and longer-term exposure to poor-quality water, the system has improved health outcomes while reducing preventable strain on services.

Time Returned, Health Improved

The benefits of clean water extend beyond health alone. Families spend less time collecting water and more time on daily activities. Schools operate more consistently, with fewer interruptions linked to water access.

For students like Tinashe and Precious, the change has been practical and immediate. With water available on site, they arrive at lessons on time, maintain hygiene with dignity, and focus on their studies rather than daily water collection. As Tinashe put it, “Now we just wake up, prepare, and go to class. We don’t worry about water anymore.”

A Foundation for the Whole Community

While the girls’ school offers a clear illustration of change, the impact of clean water is felt across Chikankata. It supports safer medical care, reduces preventable illness, strengthens education, and improves daily living conditions for families throughout the mission and surrounding community.

As the system continues to expand, clean water is becoming a foundational investment at Chikankata underpinning health, learning, and the effective functioning of services, now and into the future.

Tinashe’s Story: How Clean Water Changed Daily Health and School Attendance

Tinashe is 17 and in her final year at Chikankata Girls’ secondary school. For her, the hardest part of the old water situation was not only the time spent fetching water, but what happened after students used it. “Before the water was very brown with particles,” she said. “It had an odor.” When students drank it or bathed with it, the effects showed up quickly. “Some people would get skin reactions,” she said. “Some of the people drink the water, they would have running stomachs.”

Tinashe experienced that directly. “I have had a running stomach because of the water,” she said. At one point, she described it happening repeatedly in a single week. The result was predictable: more missed time in class, and more pressure trying to recover work later. “It made me feel bad because I missed class,” she said.

Even when she was not sick, the daily work of getting water pulled students out of the school day. Tinashe said she would almost always miss “the first and second session,” because fetching water could take “about an hour and a half,” and students had to wait their turn. “Most of the times it has delayed me for class,” she said. “By the time you come back, you find that maybe the first session is over.” Catching up was difficult. “If you lose the first explanation from a teacher, it will be hard for you to go back and study the topic yourself,” she said.

With running water now available at the school, Tinashe said, “we just wake up going to the bathroom because we have running water… prepare for class because I won’t delay.” She describes the difference as straightforward: she can attend class consistently, stay healthy, and focus on completing school well enough to pursue her next step. Her plan is to study accounting and business administration, and she talks about using those skills to help women manage budgets and resources. Without water interrupting health and attendance, her plan has become more realistic.

Precious’ Story: How Access to Safe Water Opened the Door to Education

Precious is 17, in Grade 12, and the head girl at Chikankata Girls’ Secondary School. Before water was piped into the school compound, students regularly left to fetch water before class. The journey often took over an hour, resulting in missed lessons, particularly the early teaching that new topics are built on.

“There was a time when we started a new topic in math… calculus,” Precious said. She had been fetching water and missed the first lesson. By the time she returned, the class had already moved on. “I tried to understand by myself,” she said, “but it wasn’t really working out.” She had to seek out the teacher afterward and ask for the topic to be explained again, while her classmates were already working on the next stage of the lesson.

With water available on the compound, Precious no longer misses the start of the school day. “We don’t delay for class,” she said. “The whole school program runs very well.” She is now able to attend lessons consistently from the beginning of the day.

Precious wants to become a doctor and is studying pure sciences, including chemistry, physics, and biology. Before water was available on the school compound, time spent collecting water meant missing early lessons that were difficult to recover later, particularly in subjects that build quickly. With clean running water now on site, she is able to attend class from the start of the day and remain there. She is completing her final year of secondary school and is planning to attend university, with consistent class attendance supporting that next step.

She describes her education as foundational, noting that “when you educate a girl child, you are educating a nation.” With water now available on site, girls stay in class instead of leaving to collect water, allowing learning to continue without interruption.

How the Clean Water System Works

The new water treatment system at Chikankata was designed to address both water safety and reliability. According to Aubrey Kaumba, Infrastructure Manager at Chikankata Mission, testing of the original water sources revealed serious risks. “The water showed E. coli contamination,” he said, “which means it was not safe for consumption.” Elevated mineral levels were also identified, raising concerns about longer-term health effects.

The treatment plant works by taking raw water and passing it through multiple stages designed to remove biological contamination and improve overall quality. The system treats the water before it is distributed, ensuring it is safe for drinking, cooking, washing, and medical use. Once treated, the water is pumped to storage and supplied to key facilities across the mission compound.

Today, the system provides clean water to the hospital, schools, hostels, and other Chikankata facilities. This has reduced dependence on unsafe surface sources and improved daily conditions across the site. Health staff report fewer cases of water related illness and skin irritation, and facilities are able to operate more consistently because water is reliable. Additional connections to surrounding homes are already in progress. The impact is already being felt in practical and measurable terms through safer water, fewer preventable health problems, and as a foundational service that supports healthcare delivery, education, and daily life across Chikankata.

stories.title: Reliable Power at Chikankata: When outages put lives at risk
stories.body:
Before reliable backup power was installed, electricity outages at Chikankata Mission Hospital regularly disrupted patient care. Power cuts were not occasional inconveniences. They were frequent, unpredictable, and dangerous, particularly at night and during emergencies.

When the grid failed, the consequences were immediate. In the operating theatre and intensive care unit (ICU), equipment shut down. Emergency Caesarean sections were interrupted mid procedure. Oxygen concentrators stopped. Patient monitors went dark. In critical moments, staff were forced to work without suction, lighting, or life-support equipment while trying to stabilize patients whose lives depended on continuous power. As Operating Theatre Sister Suwiranji Nareawala explained, "when the power went out, emergency operations could not continue safely. Lives were at risk, and in some cases, we lost patients."

In the ICU, electricity failures created direct risk for patients who relied on oxygen and continuous monitoring. When power went out, life-support equipment stopped working and alternatives were limited. In some emergencies, care could not be sustained long enough to save the patient. Lives were lost because electricity failed at critical moments, underscoring the essential need for reliable power. "Oxygen concentrators and monitors stopped working when the power failed. In some cases, we were racing against time, and the power did not return soon enough," said Stella Namashoba, ICU nurse at Chikankata Mission Hospital.

To keep the hospital running, diesel generators were used heavily, but they were expensive, unreliable, and difficult to sustain. Fuel shortages meant generators could not always be run continuously. Even when fuel was available, switching between grid power and generators introduced delays at precisely the moments when seconds mattered.

Installing solar power: protecting care when the grid fails

In 2024, with funding support from the Helmsley Charitable Trust, solar power was installed at Chikankata Mission Hospital to provide backup electricity during grid outages. The system operates alongside the national grid, supplying power automatically when external electricity fails. Its purpose is not to replace the grid, but to ensure that critical hospital functions remain operational during interruptions.

Previously, when grid power was interrupted, critical hospital services were disrupted. Sudden outages shut down operating theatres and intensive care equipment, forcing staff to respond to power loss while managing emergencies. Oxygen concentrators, patient monitors, suction equipment, and lighting were vulnerable to interruption, creating avoidable risk during procedures and critical care.

With the solar system now in place, essential areas of the hospital remain powered during outages. Emergency care continues without delay, surgical procedures do not need to be paused, and ICU patients remain supported throughout power interruptions. Staff no longer need to switch manually between power sources or rely on generators to sustain critical equipment, allowing care to continue safely, consistently, and without disruption.

As a result, reliable power has strengthened continuity of care at Chikankata by protecting operating theatres, intensive care, diagnostic services, and nighttime access from outages. This reduces preventable risk, supports clinical decisionmaking during emergencies, and allows services to continue without interruption when they are most needed.

What reliable power has changed for patients

The immediate impact of solar power is on patient safety:

  • Emergency surgery is now available when needed.
    Before reliable power, operating theatre use was limited to planned surgical days, typically once a week. Emergency operations, including Caesarean sections, could not be performed safely outside those windows. With reliable backup power, emergency surgeries can now take place at any time, day or night.
  • Surgeries are no longer interrupted by power outages.
    When grid power fails, lighting, suction, and monitoring remain operational. Procedures continue without sudden stops, reducing disruption during surgery and allowing patients and clinical teams to remain calm and focused.
  • ICU patients remain supported during outages.
    Patients who rely on oxygen, suction, and continuous monitoring are no longer at immediate risk when power fails. Oxygen concentrators and monitoring equipment continue operating, preventing abrupt shutdowns during critical care.
  • Emergency care at night is safer and more consistent.
    Full lighting and functional equipment remain available during outages, allowing emergencies to be managed safely without delays caused by darkness or equipment failure.
  • Clinical staff can reach the hospital safely at any hour.
    Solar street lighting across the hospital grounds allows nurses and other staff to travel to and from the hospital at night to attend to patients or carry out emergency procedures. The predominantly female staff no longer face the risks associated with walking in darkness, including fear of attack or stray dogs.
  • Delays caused by switching to generators have been eliminated.
    Care no longer depends on fuel availability or manual transitions between power sources, removing a major source of interruption during emergencies.
  • Patient care is no longer dependent on outage duration.
    Treatment can proceed continuously regardless of how long grid power is unavailable, improving safety and predictability during critical moments.

For patients and families, this has reduced fear and uncertainty during emergencies. Care is no longer dependent on whether fuel is available or how long an outage lasts.

Reduced dependence on generators and operating costs

Solar backup has also reduced the hospital's reliance on diesel generators:

  • Fuel consumption has dropped significantly
  • Generator runtime and maintenance demands have decreased
  • Funds previously spent on diesel can now be redirected to patient care, equipment, and essential supplies

While cost savings were not the primary goal, they have strengthened the hospital's ability to operate sustainably while protecting critical services.

Diagnostic care without dangerous delays

Reliable power also affects diagnostics where electricity is required to confirm injuries or complications. Previously, outages could delay imaging or force patients to travel elsewhere, sometimes over long distances, simply to confirm a diagnosis.

With consistent power, diagnostic services remain available when patients need them. Patients with injuries no longer have to postpone care or make unnecessary trips because equipment shut down unexpectedly. For patients in pain or distress, avoiding those delays reduces both risk and cost.

stories.title: A Diagnosis Without the Long Journey
stories.body:
Donate Today

For years, access to X-ray services at Chikankata Mission Hospital was uncertain. The old machine broke down frequently, often without warning. When it failed, patients waited. When it could not be repaired quickly, they traveled.

Eventually, the machine stopped working altogether. For more than a year, Chikankata had no functioning Xray equipment. Patients who needed imaging to confirm a fracture, assess an injury, or support treatment for tuberculosis were sent elsewhere. On an average day, at least 20 patients who required Xray imaging were referred out, often to Kafue or Lusaka, because diagnostic services were unavailable on site. As radiographer Mulwa Phiri explained, “that was the minimum number we were referring every day,” adding that many of those journeys were “very far and very costly for the patients.”

For patients already in pain, the journey itself was a burden. Many of those referrals were for fractures caused by road traffic and oxcart accidents, which make up the majority of Xray cases seen at the hospital. Others were for chest infections, including suspected tuberculosis, where treatment decisions depend on imaging results. For these patients, delays stretched from days into weeks, not because care was unavailable, but because diagnosis was far away.

Shelly Mainza remembers that period clearly. In 2024, she injured her back. With no Xray services available at Chikankata, she traveled repeatedly to seek care elsewhere. Each trip cost money she could not easily replace. Diagnosis and treatment took time because of the back and forth required to get the x-rays she needed elsewhere.

When Shelly returned to Chikankata in 2026 with a broken hand, the experience was completely different. Thanks to funding support from the Helmsley Charitable Trust, the hospital now had a new digital Xray machine. Her Xray was taken on site, and the image was transmitted digitally. Her Xray was taken on site, and the image was transmitted digitally. By the time she walked around the corner to the physiotherapy unit, her X-rays were already there. The injury was confirmed the same day, and treatment began immediately. The entire process, from imaging to diagnosis, was provided at no cost, eliminating the travel, delay, and expense she had faced before.

For patients, the change is immediate and practical. Injuries no longer require long journeys just to confirm what is wrong. Suspected fractures can be assessed quickly. TB patients can be diagnosed and monitored without leaving the community. Care begins sooner, and unnecessary travel is avoided.

From the hospital’s perspective, the difference is consistency. Imaging is no longer dependent on whether an aging machine is working or whether patients can afford to travel. Results are available quickly, allowing clinicians to make decisions without delay and coordinate care more effectively.

While the new Xray machine does not replace clinical expertise, it does change how quickly diagnosis can occur and where it takes place. Patients can now be assessed and treated at Chikankata without traveling elsewhere or delaying care. This provides consistent access to diagnostic imaging for injuries and for conditions such as tuberculosis, supporting both emergency decisions and ongoing treatment within the hospital.

When diagnosis happens in time

At Chikankata, the most immediate impact of the new digital Xray machine has been on patients whose care depends on timely diagnosis, particularly those with fractures and those with suspected tuberculosis.

Before the new machine was installed, most patients needing Xray imaging were referred elsewhere. According to radiography staff, road traffic and oxcart accidents account for the majority of Xray cases at the hospital. These patients often arrived in pain, with injuries that could not be safely treated without imaging. When the old machine was not working, they were sent to distant facilities, delaying treatment and increasing the risk of complications.

With digital X-ray now available on site, those patients are assessed immediately. Fractures can be confirmed the same day, allowing clinicians to immobilize injuries, begin physiotherapy, or determine whether surgical referral is needed without delay. The difference is not technological sophistication, but timing: injuries are managed before swelling worsens, before patients attempt to travel, and before untreated fractures lead to longer-term disability.

Chest infections present a similar risk when diagnosis is delayed. For patients with suspected tuberculosis, Xray imaging is often necessary to confirm disease and guide treatment decisions. In the past, these patients were also referred out when imaging was unavailable. “Some of the management depends on the Xray,” radiographer Mulwa Phiri explained, meaning treatment could not move forward without it.

Today, those patients can be imaged at Chikankata. Diagnosis and follow-up no longer depend on travel, repeated visits, or waiting for results from other facilities. Treatment decisions are made sooner, reducing the risk that illness progresses while patients wait for confirmation.

In both cases, the impact is the same: care begins when patients arrive, often within a few minutes of arriving. The digital X-ray machine has removed a critical bottleneck in diagnosis, allowing injuries and serious infections to be identified and treated before they become life-threatening.

Diagnosed in Time: How a Life-Threatening Blockage Was Identified and a Life Was Saved

Before: Before Installation of the New X-Ray Equipment and Solar Power

Before Chikankata Mission Hospital installed its new Xray machine - and before the addition of solar power - electricity outages regularly disrupted diagnostic care. During this period, imaging equipment could not be used when grid power failed.

In one such case, a member of staff was injured in a motorcycle accident and arrived at the hospital in severe pain. An Xray was required to assess the injury, but a power outage rendered the imaging equipment inoperable. The patient remained at the hospital for several hours, extending into the next day, while staff monitored their condition and managed pain, awaiting the return of electricity.

As the outage continued, clinicians reached a point where diagnosis and treatment could not safely proceed without imaging. With no reliable power and no way to complete the Xray on site, the patient was ultimately referred to another facility four hours away, without diagnostic imaging, so that care could continue.

After: When Diagnosis Happened in Time

After the installation of the new digital Xray machine, a different case showed how timely diagnosis can change outcomes. A patient arrived at Chikankata with severe symptoms that could not be explained through examination alone. Imaging was required to understand what was happening internally.

This time, Xray services were available on site. The image was taken and reviewed without delay. The results revealed a life-threatening intestinal blockage that required urgent specialist care. Because the diagnosis was made immediately, staff at Chikankata were able to act quickly and arrange referral without hesitation. The patient was transferred for treatment with a clear diagnosis in hand.

In this case, the critical difference was speed. The condition was identified before the patient deteriorated further, and referral was based on confirmed findings rather than uncertainty. The patient survived because diagnosis happened in time and staff were able to respond without delay.

Shelly’s Story: Two Accidents and Two Very Different Outcomes

Shelly Mainza has experienced both sides of care at Chikankata Mission Hospital.

In 2024, Shelly injured her back. At the time, the hospital did not have a functioning Xray machine. Imaging was required to understand the injury, but it could not be done on site. To obtain an Xray, Shelly had to travel to other facilities, including Kafue and Lusaka. Each trip took time and required money she had set aside for daily needs. Diagnosis and treatment were delayed, not because care was unavailable, but because confirmation depended on travel.

In 2026, Shelly returned to Chikankata after breaking her hand. This time, the hospital had a new digital Xray machine. Imaging was done on site. Her Xray was taken and transmitted digitally, and the results were available immediately. By the time she walked to the physiotherapy unit, her Xrays were already there. The injury was confirmed the same day, and treatment began without delay. The entire process, from imaging to diagnosis, was provided at no cost.

The difference between Shelly’s two experiences was not the injury itself. It was timely access to diagnosis and the cost of that diagnosis. In 2024, care depended on distance and the ability to travel. In 2026, diagnosis happened at the hospital when she arrived at no cost to her and allowed treatment to begin immediately.

For patients like Shelly, access to onsite diagnostic services means injuries can be assessed without delay, unnecessary travel is avoided, and care can move forward based on clinical need rather than logistics. At Chikankata, the availability of digital Xray services has changed not only how care is delivered, but when it begins.

stories.title: Chikankata Mission Hospital: Care at the Centre of Rural Zambia
stories.body:
Donate Today to Change Lives

The Salvation Army’s Chikankata Mission Hospital is located in the heart of rural southern Zambia, more than three hours by road from the capital city, Lusaka. It serves a wide and dispersed population of more than 55,000 people living across farming communities, small settlements, and mission compounds where access to services is shaped by distance, infrastructure, and seasonal conditions.

For many families, Chikankata is the only hospital they can realistically reach. Established 82 years ago at its current location, it has grown over time into a key regional institution, serving as a referral hospital for surrounding rural clinics, outreach posts, and mission schools. From its rural setting, Chikankata provides inpatient care, emergency services, and specialist referral for communities spread across a wide geographic area, many of whom would otherwise have no practical access to hospital level care.

A Long Serving Institution Responding to Aging Infrastructure

As a long-established mission hospital, Chikankata’s infrastructure reflects the period in which it was built. Core systems such as water supply, power, clinical facilities, and diagnostic services were designed decades ago for a smaller population and a more limited range of medical services. Over time, this aging infrastructure has come under increasing strain, affecting the hospital’s ability to operate reliably and safely, particularly during emergencies or periods of high demand.

In response, a series of targeted projects have been undertaken to address these constraints and ensure that Chikankata can continue to serve its community effectively. The work has been funded primarily through the Helmsley Charitable Trust, with additional support from other partners, including the Karlin Family Foundation. Together, these investments represent practical responses to specific infrastructure gaps that began to limit care delivery. Key areas of investment include:

  • Upgrading water systems, replacing reliance on unsafe surface water and ensuring reliable access for patients, staff, and schools.
  • Strengthening primary health care, through support for rural clinics and outreach services that reduce unnecessary travel and ease pressure on the hospital.
  • Improving power reliability, including partnering in installing of solar backup systems to protect critical services during frequent grid outages.
  • Enhancing diagnostic and referral capacity, allowing patients to be assessed more quickly and referred appropriately without long, costly journeys.

Explore Chikankata Stories

An Integrated Approach to Rural Care

What distinguishes Chikankata is not one project in isolation, but how water, power, diagnostic capabilities, and referral systems work together to keep the hospital functioning and responsive in a remote setting.

Clean water reduces preventable illness and supports the hospital, schools, and other services across the Chikankata compound. Hospitalsupported primary care and outreach services extend treatment into surrounding communities, reducing travel burdens for patients while maintaining clear referral pathways back to Chikankata Mission Hospital when higher-level care is needed. Reliable power allows surgeries, intensive care, and diagnostic services to continue during outages. Improved imaging and referral systems shorten waiting times, strengthen clinical decisionmaking, and reduce costs for patients.

Together, these investments address the realities of aging infrastructure while preserving Chikankata’s core purpose: providing safe, dependable care to rural communities for whom alternatives are limited or nonexistent.

Primary Health Care: Building Capacity Close to Communities

The Primary Health Care program at Chikankata was established in 2018, at a time when many rural clinics in the surrounding area were operating with extremely limited capacity. In some locations, a single nurse was responsible for all outpatient care, maternal services, and referrals, often serving large and widely dispersed populations.

The program focused on strengthening frontline services rather than replacing them. It supported rural clinics with additional community health workers, training, outreach coordination, and clear referral pathways to Chikankata Mission Hospital. Over time, this approach increased both capacity and consistency of care across the network of clinics serving the region.

Today, clinics of this type are typically staffed by five or six health workers, allowing services to be delivered more reliably and safely. Antenatal care, HIV testing and treatment, child health services, and routine outpatient care are now available closer to where people live, reducing unnecessary travel and easing pressure on the hospital.

Importantly, the systems and practices established through the Primary Health Care program have continued beyond the end of the initial Helmsley Charitable Trust project funding. Outreach services, referral protocols, and standards of care introduced in 2018 are now embedded as routine practice, continuing to shape service delivery across the community.

As a result, Primary Health Care has had a sustained impact. Patients are seen earlier, referrals are clearer and timelier, and hospital services are better able to focus on cases that require higher-level care. The program strengthened not only individual clinics, but the overall health system supporting rural communities around Chikankata.

Maternal and Child Health: A Regional Referral Hub

The Maternal and Child Health (MCH) clinic at Chikankata Mission Hospital serves as the central referral point for surrounding rural clinics and outreach posts.

The clinic provides antenatal and postnatal care, prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, child growth monitoring, family planning, and dedicated services for teenage mothers delivered in age appropriate settings. Male involvement is actively encouraged, with couples attending counselling, testing, and education together.

When complications are identified at rural clinics, patients are referred to Chikankata Hospital for ultrasound, higher-level obstetric care, or supervised delivery through a network support system. For women who live far from the hospital, a mother’s shelter near the facility allows them to stay close to care as they approach delivery, reducing risk during labor.

This referral model allows early identification of complications, timely escalation of care, and safer outcomes for mothers and children across a wide catchment area.

Reliable Power: Continuity of Care During Emergencies

In a hospital setting, electricity is essential for safe care. Prior to the installation of solar power, outages regularly disrupted services at Chikankata. Critical equipment stopped functioning, procedures were delayed, and staff were required to manage additional risk during power cuts, particularly during emergencies and at night. To maintain operations, the hospital relied heavily on diesel generators, which were costly to run and difficult to sustain over time.

Solar power was installed at the hospital in 2024, providing reliable backup power across the hospital. Since then, its impact has been felt across multiple departments. In the intensive care unit, oxygen concentrators, patient monitors, and suction equipment continue operating during grid outages. In the operating theatre, surgical procedures can proceed without interruption, even when external power fails.

Staff report reduced clinical risk, improved confidence during emergencies, and greater consistency in care delivery since the introduction of solar backup. Essential services are now protected during outages, allowing care to continue safely when it is most needed.

The introduction of solar power has also significantly reduced the hospital’s dependence on generators, lowering fuel consumption and operating costs. Resources previously spent on fuel and generator maintenance can now be redirected toward patient care, equipment, and essential services. Staff report reduced clinical risk, improved confidence during emergencies, and greater consistency in care delivery since the introduction of solar backup.

Reliable power has also improved safety beyond clinical spaces. Solar lighting allows patients, families, and staff to move safely around the hospital at night, reducing delays in seeking care and improving access during emergencies.

Diagnostics and Referral: Reducing Delay and Cost

Reliable power supports diagnostic services as well. With onsite digital X-ray and ultrasound imaging, patients no longer need to travel long distances simply to obtain a diagnosis. Waiting times are shorter, results are available quickly, and images can be shared with referral hospitals to support faster decision-making.

For patients with injuries or suspected complications, this reduces both cost and delay. One patient who fractured her arm after a fall was able to walk to Chikankata, receive an Xray and treatment the same day, and avoid days of travel and expense that had been required in the past.

Clean Water: A Foundation for Community Health

Until recently, households across the Chikankata mission and surrounding community relied on surface water sources such as the lake, as well as underground boreholes a considerable distance away. Collecting water was time-consuming and physically demanding, often requiring long walks and repeated trips each day. These demands affected families, schools, and health services alike, shaping daily routines and limiting time for work, learning, and care.

Testing of these water sources identified serious quality concerns. The water was contaminated with E. Coli, indicating fecal contamination and a high risk of waterborne disease. It was also found to contain elevated mineral levels, which can contribute to kidney-related health problems over time. These findings reflected what community members and health staff were observing in practice: frequent stomach illness, skin rashes, and irritation associated with water use, placing additional strain on households and the local health system.

Today, following the installation of a new water treatment plant in 2025, treated water is supplied to key facilities across the mission compound, including the hospital, clinics and schools, with connections to most nearby homes expected to be completed in the coming months.

Residents no longer depend on unsafe surface sources for drinking, washing, or cooking in areas already connected to the new system, or have to walk long distances to collect water from boreholes. Early monitoring and reports from health staff indicate significant reductions in waterborne illness, skin irritation, and hygiene related complaints, reflecting improved water quality and safer daily use.

The impact is both immediate and cumulative. Families spend less time collecting water and more time on other daily activities, while health facilities report fewer cases of water-borne illness requiring treatment. Schools and other community services are operating more consistently, with fewer disruptions linked to water access. By addressing both biological contamination, including E. Coli, water-borne parasites like amoebas, dangerous viruses such as typhoid, and elevated mineral levels, the water system has improved safety while reducing longer-term health risks linked to untreated sources.

Clean water has become a foundational investment at Chikankata, supporting community health, education, and the effective functioning of services across the mission as system coverage continues to expand.

stories.title: The Salvation Army Activates Early Prevention Measures to Support Communities in Eastern DRC
stories.body:
Donate Now

Update: June 5, 2026

Why Faith-Based Organizations Are Critical to the Ebola Response in the Democratic Republic of Congo

As the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) confronts a new Ebola outbreak, the global response faces a familiar challenge: how to reach communities quickly with accurate information and lifesaving care, in a context shaped by conflict, displacement, and deep-rooted mistrust.

With no vaccine or treatment available, prevention is critical to stopping the spread. At its core, this is about trust as much as medicine.

Recent analysis from frontline experts underscores a key reality. In the absence of widely available vaccines or treatments, containing Ebola depends on how quickly health workers can identify cases, isolate infections, and engage communities with credible, trusted information.

In this environment, faith-based organizations play a decisive, frontline role.

A Network That Already Exists

The Salvation Army has operated in the DRC for more than 90 years, building a nationwide presence rooted in local communities. Today, that includes:

  • 496 schools
  • 29 health centers
  • 319 corps and outposts, alongside community and care facilities

This network is long established, locally led, and embedded in the communities it serves. As a result of decades of consistent presence, The Salvation Army and its staff are widely known and trusted. The Salvation Army’s officers, teachers, and health workers are seen as insiders, who are part of everyday community life, known by name, working in familiar places, and present long before the current crisis began, and long after crises end.

Why Trust Determines Whether Outbreaks Are Contained

The importance of this local presence is well documented. Ebola response efforts in the DRC have repeatedly been undermined by mistrust of external organizations.

During the 2018–2020 outbreak, more than 450 incidents of violence or threats against health workers were recorded, driven in part by distrust of outside-led interventions and top-down communication approaches. Research and field reporting show that communities often resisted interventions when they felt excluded, misunderstood, or disconnected from decision-making.

At the same time, faith leaders and local organizations played a critical role in bridging this gap. They helped counter misinformation, explain public health measures, and restore confidence in the response.

Current expert guidance emphasizes that community trust, local leadership, and long-term presence remain essential to an effective Ebola response.

Trusted People Deliver Trusted Information

One of the most consistent lessons from previous Ebola outbreaks is that messages are only effective when they come from trusted sources. During the 2018–2020 crisis:

  • Faith leaders and teachers were trained to deliver Ebola prevention messages
  • These trusted community figures reached hundreds of thousands of people with accurate information
  • Their involvement helped reduce stigma and improve community acceptance

This is critical in a disease outbreak where misinformation can spread as quickly as the virus itself.

Faith-based organizations operate within existing social structures. Their leaders are already part of daily life, including worship, education, and community decision-making. As a result, they can communicate in ways that are culturally relevant and credible.

The Role of Local Institutions in Access and Acceptance

Ebola does not spread through casual contact. It spreads through direct interaction with infected individuals or contaminated surfaces. That makes early detection and behavior change essential. But both depend on access and acceptance. Faith-based organizations help address both:

  • Access: Schools, clinics, and corps buildings serve as established points for outreach, training, and service delivery
  • Acceptance: Communities are more likely to engage with services provided by institutions they already trust

This is especially important in regions affected by conflict, where mobility is limited and external actors may face barriers to entry.

The Salvation Army’s Role in Previous Ebola Responses

The Salvation Army’s work during prior outbreaks demonstrates the practical impact of this model. In North Kivu, the organization worked with:

  • 10 health centers
  • 320 schools
  • 120 faith-based institutions

to deliver hygiene training and prevention messaging.

Local leaders were trained and then equipped to train others, creating a multiplier effect that extended far beyond the initial intervention. The organization also supported:

  • Installation of handwashing infrastructure in schools and community locations
  • Provision of protective equipment for clinics
  • Community-level education programs to reduce stigma and misinformation

This approach leveraged existing relationships rather than attempting to build new ones during the crisis.

Faith-Based Organizations in Today’s Response

The current outbreak presents similar challenges to those seen in previous crises:

  • Fragile health systems
  • Ongoing conflict and insecurity
  • Population movement across regions
  • Limited treatment options

In this context, organizations with deep local roots are uniquely positioned to act quickly and effectively. Faith-based organizations provide:

  • Continuity: They remain in place before, during, and after crises
  • Credibility: Their long-standing presence builds trust over time
  • Reach: Their networks extend into remote and underserved areas
  • Inclusivity: They serve all people, regardless of background or status

The Salvation Army’s approach reflects this. Its officers and staff are part of the communities they serve, known for welcoming all.

A Critical Component of an Effective Response

Ebola outbreaks cannot be contained through clinical interventions alone. They require:

  • Community engagement
  • Behavior change
  • Trust in public health guidance
  • Local leadership

Faith-based organizations are essential to each of these elements. As global health partners mobilize resources and technical expertise, the role of embedded, trusted organizations on the ground remains indispensable. In the DRC, that includes a network of faith-based organizations, including The Salvation Army, built over decades that continue to serve as a foundation for response, resilience, and recovery. The DRC government is also working closely with the faith community to support risk communication and community engagement to combat the current outbreak.

Update: June 1, 2026

Salvation Army Ebola Response Expands in Ituri and Across Democratic Republic of the Congo

The Salvation Army’s response to the Ebola crisis is continuing to scale in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, with activity now centered in Bunia, Ituri province, one of the outbreak’s epicenters.

In Bunia, The Salvation Army is actively participating in coordination meetings led by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), contributing to local response planning alongside government and humanitarian partners. The corps is also mobilizing community volunteers to support outreach and assistance to affected populations.

Two emergency projects are now moving forward:

  • Community-based prevention and awareness efforts targeting households in villages around Bunia, focused on Ebola symptoms, transmission, alert systems, and hygiene practices, alongside the distribution of sanitation materials.
  • Support to frontline health workers in North and South Kivu, including the provision of personal protective equipment (PPE), where partners report that existing supplies remain insufficient to meet demand.

The Salvation Army’s medical leadership is also directly engaged in Ministry of Health planning efforts, ensuring alignment with government-led response strategies. In Kinshasa, The Salvation Army Territorial Headquarters is convening faith-based networks in partnership with the Ministry of Health to strengthen risk communication and community engagement. This includes addressing misinformation, building trust, and promoting critical prevention behaviors such as handwashing, patient isolation, and safe, dignified burials, particularly important in communities where confidence in public authorities remains low.

Working with health authorities and partners, The Salvation Army is advancing prevention, hygiene, and community-based response efforts to reduce the risk of Ebola transmission.

The Salvation Army is working in coordination with national health authorities and international partners to support early response efforts in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Drawing on experience from previous outbreak responses, teams are focused on prevention, community engagement, and strengthening frontline capacity to reduce the risk of transmission and protect vulnerable populations.

Coordinated Response and Local Capacity

The Salvation Army is part of ongoing coordination efforts with the DRC Ministry of Health and other partners, supporting a unified and locally led response. Through its established presence across the country—including health facilities, schools, and community centers—the organization is positioned to contribute to prevention and response activities.

This network enables work with trusted community leaders, including officers, teachers, and local personnel, to share accurate information and support community-level engagement.

Prevention and Hygiene Interventions

Early actions are focused on reducing transmission risk through proven public health measures, including:

  • Activation of hygiene protocols across Salvation Army facilities
  • Expansion of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions
  • Preparation for distribution of personal protective equipment (PPE), handwashing materials, and infection prevention supplies

These measures are informed by established public health approaches and prior outbreak responses.

Supporting Frontline Workers and Communities

As response efforts are prepared to scale, if needed, The Salvation Army is taking steps to support:

  • Healthcare and community workers with protective equipment and supplies
  • Continued access to safe hygiene and sanitation resources
  • Community-based efforts that help individuals understand and reduce risk

Work is also underway to strengthen infection prevention measures across Salvation Army-supported locations to ensure services can continue safely.

Community Engagement and Risk Communication

A key focus of the response is working through trusted local networks to support community understanding and participation.

This includes:

  • Training community members and personnel in awareness and prevention practices
  • Supporting communication efforts that are clear, accurate, and locally relevant
  • Engaging leaders in culturally sensitive areas—including care practices and burial traditions—to help reduce risk while respecting local context

These efforts help families continue daily life while reducing fear and preventing further spread.

Building on Experience

The Salvation Army’s team in the DRC has prior experience responding to Ebola outbreaks, including the 2018–2020 response. This experience is informing current planning and early action.

Efforts are being developed across two areas:

  • Rapid response support, including immediate supply and prevention measures
  • Strengthening health systems, with a focus on improving long-term preparedness and infection control

Updates will be shared as more information becomes available through verified partner and public health sources.

stories.title: How a Community Led Vision in Guatemala Transformed Tecpán's Soccer Field
stories.body:
What began as a simple dirt lot in Tecpán, Guatemala, a patch of ground where children played barefoot and community members gathered informally, has grown into one of the region’s most inspiring examples of locally driven development.

Families in the area long hoped for a safe, modern space where their children could play after school, build confidence, and stay active. When The Salvation Army listened to that vision, the transformation began. The dusty field was rebuilt into a durable synthetic soccer field, giving young people a safe, high quality place to call their own.

But the field presented other opportunities. Instead of just becoming a resource for youth. It also became a lifeline for the whole community – and local corps.

A local market study indicated that the location of the field gave it strong business potential. There is no comparable center in Tecpán offering the same blend of sports facilities, lodging, and event spaces. The Salvation Army World Service Office (SAWSO) helped support its transition from a simple after school gathering space to a community business venture with sustainable impact.

Today, the refurbished soccer field stands as a high demand, revenue generating community asset. Children continue to use the field during after school hours as originally intended, but it is now also rented to adults in the evenings. This arrangement meets a substantial community need for recreational facilities while creating a reliable income stream. The shared use model allows the Guatemala based center to move closer to self sustainability, helping cover operational costs and ensuring that both the field and the programs connected to it can thrive for years to come.

Every weekday from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m., the field remains fully booked. Its popularity has made it one of the center’s most consistent sources of income, along with lodging, social event rentals, independently managed snack bar operations, and four on site rooms leased to local organizations. These combined revenue streams support maintenance, strengthen programming, and improve the long-term viability of the Tecpán center.

The field has proven so popular that there is now a growing need to renovate additional building space and expand lodging capacity in order to accommodate the steady flow of visitors drawn to both the soccer field and other camp activities.

What was once a humble dirt patch now positions The Salvation Army’s Guatemala property as a unique hub for community connection, recreation, and sustainable impact. From its origins as a simple request from families who wanted a better place for their children to play, the Tecpán soccer field has become a broader story of resilience, ownership, and community hope. It reflects a place where local dreams created the foundation for long term sustainability and a brighter future for Guatemala’s youth.

stories.title: Powering Hope: How Solar Energy is Transforming Communities in Guatemala
stories.body:
Powering Hope: How Solar Energy is Transforming Communities in Guatemala

In the highlands of Guatemala, where families often struggle to make ends meet, schools and community centers face a harsh reality: rising energy costs and limited resources threaten their ability to provide education and safe spaces for children. For many, the choice is stark: Pay the electric bill or invest in better classrooms. Without intervention, these schools risk falling behind, leaving seats empty and futures uncertain.

The Challenge

Electricity is expensive, and in rural areas, power outages are common. Schools like Maya and Tierra Nueva were spending a significant portion of their limited budgets on energy, leaving little for teacher salaries, learning materials, or extracurricular programs. At Tecpán Camp, a vital hub for youth retreats and community events, the cost of utilities was eating into funds that could have supported expansion and maintenance.

The Solution: Solar Power

Through SAWSO's Developing Financial Independence (DIF) initiative, solar panel projects were introduced in schools and at Tecpán Camp. These installations do more than keep the lights on. They also slash energy costs, freeing up funds for critical needs like teacher pay and classroom improvements.

Captain Cristina Cedillo, who along with her husband leads the Chimaltenango Corps and school, shares:

"We are working with 172 kids in Pre-school and elementary school. In the school, we were part of a project in which solar panels were installed. Prior to the solar panels, we paid a bill of 1,900 Quetzales - the highest. Now we are paying 150–300 Quetzales, which is a significant reduction, helping us a lot with covering operations costs and a bit of remodeling within the school, which are noticeable - they're visible."


How It Generates Opportunity

Solar energy also expands opportunity. Lower operating costs mean schools can offer new programs, like music bands and after-school activities, attracting more students and increasing enrollment fees. At Tecpán Camp, savings from solar power help fund upgrades that make the camp more appealing for events, boosting rental income. These changes turn sustainability into a revenue engine, ensuring that every dollar saved is a dollar reinvested in education and community growth.

Captain Cedillo adds:

"With the funds we've saved with our reduced light bill, we've accomplished changing the playhouse for the kids. In addition, we've successfully paved a part of the field that, in the future, we hope to turn into a beautiful field for the kids."


The Impact

In classrooms once at risk of closing and community spaces that faced uncertain futures, hope now shines bright - quite literally. Solar panels have transformed schools and camps across Guatemala, turning financial strain into opportunity. Teachers enjoy greater stability, students thrive in enriched programs, and families see a future filled with promise.

Parents proudly watch their children march in school bands, and Tecpán Camp is fully booked for retreats and celebrations. What began as a sustainability effort has become a movement of empowerment, proving that even in the most vulnerable areas, innovation can light the way to lasting change.

stories.title: Rebuilding Education and Stability in the Pool Region, Republic of Congo
stories.body:
For more than 25 years, the Pool Region of the Republic of Congo experienced recurring political conflict that disrupted community life, weakened social cohesion, and severely damaged the education system. Although open hostilities ended in 2016, the effects remain. Many of the region's 437,000 residents still face limited economic opportunity, intermittent social unrest, and a scarcity of reliable public services.

Educational Conditions Today

Access to quality education remains one of the most significant challenges. Many communities lack functioning school buildings, trained teachers, and basic instructional materials. School fees are often too high for families living in poverty. Teacher absenteeism is common, and some schools operate with only one teacher for multiple grade levels.

Surveys conducted in project communities indicate that up to half of all children never enroll in school, and many who do attend only sporadically. Outside of a few textbooks, reading materials are generally unavailable in both schools and homes. These education barriers exist alongside broader needs for safe water, sanitation, and stable community spaces.

The Salvation Army's Role

Armée du Salut (ADS), The Salvation Army in the Republic of Congo, operates a network of churches (“Corps”) across the Pool Region. These locations are well-established, trusted by local leaders, and often serve as neutral gathering spaces in communities that have experienced conflict. Because of these relationships, ADS Corps sites are practical and secure places to launch community-based development initiatives.

About the Project

SAWSO, in partnership with ADS and several technical organizations, is implementing a three-year pilot project: Building Community Resilience through Education and Peacebuilding Initiatives.

The project focuses on improving basic literacy, strengthening community connections, and addressing the ongoing psychological impacts of conflict. It does so by establishing Community Learning Centers (CLCs) at up to six Salvation Army Corps locations.

Its objectives include:

1. Basic Literacy Development

  • Teaching foundational reading and writing skills in the local Lari language, with gradual introduction of French.
  • Providing literacy support for out-of-school children and youth to help them enter or re-enter formal schooling.
  • Reinforcing classroom learning for students who are already enrolled.

2. Availability of Reading Materials

  • Supplying printed and digital books, phonics tools, visual aids, and locally appropriate children's stories.
  • Using the Bloom online library to adapt and create new materials in Lari.

3. Psycho-Social Support and Community Stability

  • Providing group counseling sessions for individuals affected by trauma, especially youth vulnerable to recruitment by armed groups.
  • Supporting structured dialogue sessions with elders, youth leaders, and women to resolve local problems and strengthen social cohesion.
  • Offering organized sports clubs (football, basketball, and ndzango) linked to life-skills education.

4. Essential Infrastructure Improvements

  • Each center includes a sheltered open-air learning space and a small library room.
  • They also have solar power, lighting, WiFi connectivity, a projector, and a laptop so children can access educational materials online given the absence of books.
  • The project also includes the construction of latrines, drilled boreholes for clean water, and playground spaces to help with hygiene.

As of November 2025, three centers have been constructed. The remaining centers will be built in 2026. A phased construction approach allows staff to learn from early sites and improve programming as new centers open.

Each center is overseen by a local management committee, ensuring community ownership. Paid teachers, supported by trained volunteers, run the literacy programs.

Project Partners

To strengthen program quality, SAWSO and ADS are working with:

  • SIL Congo, which designs the literacy curriculum and trains teachers and volunteers.
  • A reading specialist consultant who builds SIL staff capacity.
  • Gothia, a nonprofit organization leading youth sports and life-skills training.
  • A Brazzaville-based organization (TBD) that will oversee trauma counseling.

Looking Ahead

By 2028, the goal is for the Community Learning Centers to operate independently under local management. Corps communities will fund ongoing teacher positions, while volunteer instructors trained during the project will mentor new volunteers.

As capacity increases, the program can extend literacy activities into nearby villages using a mobile model that requires only books and basic supplies. The centers can also support future community development activities as the model expands to additional Salvation Army locations across the Pool Region.

Our Impact

The Pool Region of the Republic of Congo experienced more than 25 years of intermittent conflict, leaving many schools without teachers, materials, or functioning facilities.

In some communities, up to 50% of children have never enrolled in school, and many who do attend only sporadically.

Before this project, most villages had no access to children's reading materials beyond a single shared textbook.

Community Learning Centers established by Armée du Salut now provide solar-powered learning spaces, digital tools, and locally developed reading resources in the Lari language.

Did You Know?

In 2025, three Community Learning Centers were completed and equipped with solar power, latrines, and borehole wells with SAWSO's support.

stories.title: Strengthening Early Childhood Education in Rwanda
stories.body:
In Rubuye, Rwanda, a coordinated early‑learning initiative is improving the quality and safety of preschool education across 11 underserved communities. An initial assessment identified significant gaps: untrained teaching staff, unregistered centers, inadequate and unsafe facilities, limited inclusion for children with disabilities, lack of child‑sized furniture, and unstructured meal preparation.

To address these needs, The Salvation Army U.S. East, SAWSO, and the Rwanda and Burundi Territory partnered with parents, Parent Teacher Associations, and the local government to upgrade the infrastructure and strengthen school management. The project resulted in safer classrooms, 20 trained early childhood education teachers, and a new selection of age‑appropriate furniture. It also created inclusive learning spaces, and introduced standardized feeding systems that meet basic health and safety requirements.

More than 300 children now attend preschools in Rwanda that meet minimum standards for learning, protection, and development. Improved attendance and classroom readiness indicate early gains in educational outcomes. The Rubuye Preschool Project demonstrates how targeted investment, supported by community ownership and local‑government engagement, can build durable improvements in early‑childhood systems.

OUR IMPACT

  • 11 preschools saw improvements to their facilities and management systems.
  • 20 teachers were trained in early childhood education methodologies.
  • 300+ children are now enrolled in safe, age‑appropriate learning environments.
  • Inclusive classrooms were established to support children with disabilities.
  • Standardized feeding programs were introduced, improving nutrition and safety.

stories.title: After the Storm: A Farmer's Fight to Feed Her Family
stories.body:
When Hurricane Melissa crushed the farmland of western Jamaica, destroying crops, livestock, and the small shop she depended on, Cordeline's life changed overnight. A farmer, who once grew everything her family ate, is now forced to rely on distributions of food and bottled water as The Salvation Army delivers relief across the devastated parishes.

"Our farm fed us."

Before Hurricane Melissa, Cordeline's days followed the rhythm of her farm. The land provided nearly everything her family needed.

"We plant sorrel and pumpkin and yam and other things. Our farm fed us. Before the hurricane I never used to buy any of the vegetables or yam from anybody else. I could go to the coop and catch the chicken and cook them. And then we had plantain and banana."

Cordeline preferred to eat only what came from her own soil. The chickens in the coop supplied meat when needed, and the plantain and banana trees filled out the rest. Even her sugar cane, once several acres, was part of a reliable cycle of harvest, sale, and home use.

Farming wasn't simply work for her; it was the structure of her independence. She rarely needed to buy food. Her farm fed her family, supported her small shop, and kept her self-sufficient. Her only outside income was from teaching English to the young people in her community.

"There's nothing left. Everything went."

When Hurricane Melissa arrived, that world ended overnight. Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica with catastrophic force. The storm leveled homes, uprooted trees, wiped out crops, and destroyed entire agricultural communities. When the winds finally stopped, Cordeline stepped outside into a changed world.

"The hurricane came and there's nothing left, everything went. After that happened I felt so bad. I was just looking at it not saying anything because there was nothing to say."

Her shop, her main source of income, was gone. "When I looked at the front of the yard the shop was not there. It was nothing - just rubble."

She describes it plainly. "There's nothing left. Everything went." When she stepped outside, she saw what the storm had taken without ceremony. The chicken coop had disappeared entirely. "I was wondering where the chickens went," she says. The cane fields were flattened. The fruit trees around the house, six large ones, plus ten coconut trees, lay snapped or uprooted.

"I felt as if I was alone in the world."

In the first days after the storm, she tried to manage with what little was left, cooking small amounts of whatever she had. But the loss of the farm meant the loss of her food, and prices in the shops rose quickly.

"We don't have any food now. There is nothing for us to eat. Drinking water is very scarce. I had to try to buy. And the prices went up so high I could not afford it. We don't have any food now. There is nothing for us to eat."

It was also a period of deep isolation. With roads blocked and communication down, many people simply disappeared from contact. "I felt as if I was alone in the world," she recalls. "There is nobody. I did not cry but the tears were right behind my eyes. I said, where is everybody? I cannot call anybody. Nobody can call me. They don't know if I'm still alive."

Days passed before some communities were reachable. She recalls a young man nearby who wasn't found for days. Some communities were so isolated that even the dead could not be reached. "Bodies could not be removed…, they had to bury them in the same place," she says.

She Stood in Line for Food and Water

It was during this time when her own resources were exhausted, that The Salvation Army began calling residents to distribution points. She describes going only because there is no longer another option. "Otherwise, I wouldn't be here," she says. "That's not me." But the need was real. She collected food parcels, drinking water, and clothing. When cooked meals were available, she brought them home to share with her family. These distributions became part of how she and her children managed from week to week.

The support has been steady: food parcels, hot meals during the early weeks, bottled water when the community supply failed, and basic items to get through each day. It hasn't restored the farm, that will take time, but it has sustained the household through months of uncertainty. "When The Salvation Army gets things, they call us," she says simply.

Even so, she speaks about the help with mixed feelings. Her independence has shaped her whole life. Accepting assistance feels unfamiliar, even uncomfortable. "I am more like an independent person who helps myself," she admits. But after listing all she has lost, she adds, "I will take the food and the water."

The Salvation Army has reached more than 212,000 people across Jamaica since Hurricane Melissa, providing steady relief to families who lost homes, crops, and access to clean water. Teams have distributed 131,000 meal kits, 66,000 hot meals, 9,000 food parcels, and more than 27,000 bottles of drinking water, along with 25,000 hygiene kits to communities facing severe shortages. These resources have helped stabilize households whose farms, shops, and livelihoods were wiped out by the storm. For many families like Cordeline's, these distributions have become a vital lifeline as they begin the long process of recovery.

She Hopes to Rebuild her Farm

Her home still needs repair; pieces of the roof continue to fall. The remaining acre of cane may or may not produce a harvest this year. She hopes for support to rebuild the farm - "to bring things to harvest" - but she knows that will come slowly.

For now, she continues forward in the same steady way she recounts her story. The land she depended on for a lifetime can no longer feed her. Until it can, she stands quietly among her neighbors, receiving supplies that help her family manage one week at a time.

It is not the life she lived before the storm. But it is the life she has learned to piece together after it.
